page.text: Build the arena and read its components
You will place a floor and four walls by exact numbers, then look inside them. Reading an object’s components is how you find out what it can do, and how you will fix almost every problem this term.

The numbers come from the same arithmetic as last week. A Cube is 1 unit tall at Scale 1, and Position is its center. The Floor has Scale Y of 1, so its center sits at Y of -0.5 and its top face is at Y of 0. The walls are 2 units tall, so their center is at Y of 1 and they stand on the floor. Wall_North and Wall_South are 22 long, so they cover the corners that Wall_East and Wall_West leave open.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**.
Type Floor and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, in the **Transform** section, set **Position** to 0, -0.5, 0. A new object appears wherever the Scene view is looking, so always type all three numbers.

shot.alt: Floor Transform: Position 0, -0.5, 0; Rotation 0, 0, 0; Scale 20, 1, 20.
shot.caption: Floor’s Transform once Position and Scale are both typed in.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Floor, Transform section only, with Position 0, -0.5, 0 and Scale 20, 1, 20 visible. Outline the Position and Scale rows.

items.text: Set **Scale** to 20, 1, 20. Leave **Rotation** at 0, 0, 0.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_North and press Enter.
Set **Position** to 0, 1, 10.5 and **Scale** to 22, 2, 1.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_South and press Enter.
Set **Position** to 0, 1, -10.5 and **Scale** to 22, 2, 1.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_East and press Enter.
Set **Position** to 10.5, 1, 0 and **Scale** to 1, 2, 20.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_West and press Enter.
Set **Position** to -10.5, 1, 0 and **Scale** to 1, 2, 20.
In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Main Camera**.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 16, -16 and **Rotation** to 45, 0, 0.
Click the **Game** tab. In the bar along its top, open the third dropdown, which reads **Free Aspect** in a new project, and choose **16:9 Aspect**.
Choose **File > Save**.

shot.alt: Game view of a gray-white floor ringed by four walls, with the Hierarchy listing Floor, Wall_North, Wall_South, Wall_East and Wall_West.
shot.caption: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect: the whole floor and all four walls are in view.
shot.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect showing the whole arena from above and in front, all objects the default gray-white. Hierarchy visible at left with Floor and the four walls listed.

page.title: Shortcut
page.text: To save time, click Wall_North and choose Edit > Duplicate (Ctrl+D on Windows, Command+D on a Mac), then choose Edit > Rename, type the new name, press Enter and change its numbers. A duplicate keeps every component of the original.
Now look inside. Everything you just made is a stack of components, and the Inspector lists them from the top.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Floor**.

In the **Inspector**, find its four components: **Transform**, **Cube (Mesh Filter)**, **Box Collider** and **Mesh Renderer**. At the bottom is the material, **Lit (Material)**, grayed out because the default material cannot be edited.

shot.alt: Inspector for Floor listing Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer and Box Collider, with Lit (Material) grayed out below and the Add Component button at the bottom.
shot.caption: Floor in the Inspector. Each outlined heading is one component.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Floor with all four component headings visible, Mesh Renderer and Box Collider included. Outline the checkbox beside Mesh Renderer.

items.text: Untick the checkbox at the left of the **Mesh Renderer** heading. The floor vanishes from the Scene view and the Game view.
Tick the checkbox again. The floor comes back.
Click the **Add Component** button, type Rigidbody, and press **Escape** to close the box without adding anything. Floor stays as it is.

page.title: Why this matters
page.text: The Mesh Filter holds the shape, the Mesh Renderer draws it, and the Box Collider is the solid shape that physics uses. You switched off the drawing and nothing else changed, so appearance and solidity are separate jobs. A Floor does not need a Rigidbody, because it should never move.

The Game view shows the whole floor and all four walls, still in plain gray-white, from above and in front. Floor is switched on again: its Mesh Renderer box is ticked. It went wrong if part of the arena is cut off (check the camera Position and Rotation), if a wall floats or sinks into the floor (check its Position Y is 1) or if the floor is missing (tick the Mesh Renderer).

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
A wall is in the wrong place: you probably typed only one Position number. Type X, Y and Z every time, because a new object does not start at 0, 0, 0.

There is a gap at a corner: Wall_North and Wall_South need Scale X of 22, not 20.

The Game view looks different from this page: set the aspect dropdown in the Game view to 16:9 Aspect and check that the camera numbers match.
Color the arena with materials
Plain gray makes every surface look the same, and the default material cannot be edited. A material of your own lets you choose a color, and one material can be shared by many objects.

A new material uses the shader Universal Render Pipeline/Lit. A shader is the small program that decides how light falls on a surface. In this shader the color of a material is the color box beside **Base Map**. There is no field called Albedo or Color. You will make four materials with these colors:

items: M_Floor, hexadecimal 3B4A5A (a dark slate)
M_Wall, hexadecimal 9AA5B1 (a light gray-blue)
M_Ramp, hexadecimal F2B134 (a warm yellow)
M_Ball, hexadecimal E8503A (a bright red-orange)

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Assets** folder.
Choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Materials and press Enter.
Double-click the **Materials** folder to open it.
Choose **Assets > Create > Material**, type M_Floor and press Enter.
With M_Floor selected, in the **Inspector** find **Surface Inputs** and click the color box beside **Base Map**.

shot.alt: Surface Inputs section of M_Floor: Base Map with a color box beside it, then Metallic Map, Smoothness 0.5, Normal Map.
shot.caption: M_Floor in the Inspector: the color box beside Base Map, and Smoothness below it.
shot.shows: The Inspector for M_Floor with Surface Inputs open. Outline the color box beside Base Map.

items.text: In the window titled **Color**, click the **Hexadecimal** box, type 3B4A5A and press Enter. Close the window.

shot.alt: Color window with the Hexadecimal box set to 3B4A5A and the R, G, B, A sliders beside it.
shot.caption: The Color window with 3B4A5A typed into the Hexadecimal box.
shot.shows: The Color window opened from the Base Map box, with the mode showing RGB 0-255 and the Hexadecimal box containing 3B4A5A. Outline the Hexadecimal box.

items.text: Make three more materials the same way: M_Wall with 9AA5B1, M_Ramp with F2B134 and M_Ball with E8503A. Each time choose **Assets > Create > Material** first.
Select M_Ball and drag the **Smoothness** slider to 0.8 so it looks shiny.
Drag M_Floor from the **Project** window onto **Floor** in the **Hierarchy**.
Drag M_Wall from the **Project** window onto **Wall_North** in the **Hierarchy**, then onto **Wall_South**, **Wall_East** and **Wall_West** in turn.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.text: The floor is a dark slate and the four walls are a lighter gray-blue. The Materials folder holds M_Floor, M_Wall, M_Ramp and M_Ball. Click Floor: the material at the bottom of its Inspector now reads M_Floor and is no longer grayed out. It went wrong if everything is still gray (the drag missed the object, so drop it on the name in the Hierarchy).

page.alt: Slate floor and gray-blue walls in the Game view; the Materials folder lists M_Floor, M_Wall, M_Ramp and M_Ball.
page.caption: Slate floor, gray-blue walls, and the four materials in the Materials folder.
page.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect with the slate floor and gray-blue walls, and the Project window beside it open on the Materials folder showing the four materials.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The color did not change: you clicked a different box. Use the color box beside Base Map, under Surface Inputs.

The Color window has no Hexadecimal box: make the window taller, or check the mode dropdown reads RGB 0-255.

Only one wall changed color: drag the material onto each wall in turn, or select all four walls in the Hierarchy with Ctrl (Windows) or Command (Mac) held and drag once.
Light the arena
A light is a component too, and it has a color of its own. What you see is the surface color and the light color together, so you will tint the light and watch every surface change.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Directional Light**.
In the **Inspector**, find the **Light** component. It has four sections that open with a triangle: **General**, **Emission**, **Rendering** and **Shadows**.
Click the triangle beside **Emission** to open it.
Find **Light Appearance**, which reads **Filter and Temperature**. Open its dropdown and choose **Color**.

shot.alt: Emission section of the Directional Light: Light Appearance set to Color, a color box, and Intensity 2.
shot.caption: The Directional Light with Light Appearance set to Color. The color box is orange for the test in the next steps.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Directional Light with the Emission section open. Outline the Light Appearance dropdown showing Color and the color box.

items.text: Click the color box that now shows in the **Emission** section.
In the window titled **Color**, click the **Hexadecimal** box, type FF8A1F and press Enter. Look at the Game view: every surface turns orange.

shot.alt: Arena tinted orange by the Directional Light set to FF8A1F: the floor and walls all look orange-brown.
shot.caption: One orange light tints every surface.
shot.shows: The Game view beside the Color window at the moment the light is FF8A1F, so the orange tint on the floor and walls is visible.

items.text: Click the color box again, type FFF4E0 in the **Hexadecimal** box and press Enter. The light is now a gentle warm white.
Check that **Intensity** reads 2 and leave it there.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: Why the orange test
page.text: You changed one number on one light and every material looked different. Light color multiplies surface color, so a slate floor under an orange light is a warm dark color. That is why games change the mood of a whole scene by changing the lights alone.

The floor and walls look like their material colors with a slight warm cast, and the walls cast shadows across the floor. The Light Appearance reads Color and Intensity reads 2. It went wrong if the arena is still orange (repeat the color step with FFF4E0) or if no color box shows (Light Appearance is still Filter and Temperature).

page.alt: The lit arena in the Game view; the Directional Light shows Light Appearance Color and Intensity 2.
page.caption: The arena under the warm white light, with the walls’ shadows on the floor.
page.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect with the lit arena, and the Inspector beside it on Directional Light with Emission open.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
You cannot find the color box: open the Emission section with its triangle, then set Light Appearance to Color.

Nothing changed in the Game view: check you selected Directional Light, not Main Camera.

The scene is far too dark or too bright: set Intensity back to 2.
Make the ball and the ramp, and add a Rigidbody
A Rigidbody is the component that lets physics move an object. You will first see a ball that does nothing, then add the Rigidbody and watch gravity and the ramp do the work.

The ramp is a Cube tilted 20 degrees. A positive Rotation X tips its far end, the +Z end, downward, so a ball landing on it rolls towards Wall_North. The Ramp is 10 long and 0.4 thick, centered at Y of 2, so its low end sits just above the floor and its high end is near 4. The ball starts at Y of 6, a little above the high part, so it falls onto the ramp.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube** and type Ramp.
Set **Position** to 0, 2, -4, **Rotation** to 20, 0, 0 and **Scale** to 6, 0.4, 10.
Drag M_Ramp from the **Materials** folder onto **Ramp** in the **Hierarchy**.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Sphere** and type Ball.

shot.alt: Yellow Ramp tilted down towards the far wall with the red-orange Ball above it; Hierarchy lists Ramp and Ball.
shot.caption: The Scene view once Ramp and Ball are both placed: the ball hangs above the high end of the ramp.
shot.shows: The Scene view with Ramp and Ball placed above it, the Ramp tilted, and the Hierarchy listing Ramp and Ball. Outline the Ball above the high part of the Ramp.

items.text: Set **Position** to 0, 6, -7 and leave **Scale** at 1, 1, 1.
Drag M_Ball from the **Materials** folder onto **Ball** in the **Hierarchy**.
With **Ball** selected, look at the **Inspector**: it has **Transform**, **Sphere (Mesh Filter)**, **Sphere Collider** and **Mesh Renderer**, but no Rigidbody.
Click the **Play** button at the top center of the Editor. The ball hangs in the air and nothing moves. Click **Play** again to stop.
Click **Add Component**, type Rigidbody and choose **Rigidbody** from the list, not Rigidbody 2D.

shot.alt: Ball Inspector: Sphere Collider, then Rigidbody with Mass 1, Linear Damping 0, Angular Damping 0.05, Use Gravity ticked.
shot.caption: Ball in the Inspector with its new Rigidbody at the bottom.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Ball after Add Component, with the Rigidbody section open and Sphere Collider above it. Outline the Rigidbody heading, Mass and Use Gravity.

items.text: Look at the new **Rigidbody** section: **Mass** 1, **Linear Damping** 0, **Angular Damping** 0.05 and **Use Gravity** ticked.
Click **Play**. The ball falls onto the ramp, rolls down, crosses the floor and stops at Wall_North. Click **Play** again to stop.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.alt: First the ball stays still in the air. After a Rigidbody is added, it falls onto the ramp, rolls down, crosses the floor and stops at the far wall.
page.caption: The same scene twice: first with no Rigidbody on Ball, then with one.
page.shows: The Game view and the top of the Editor so the Play button is visible. First press Play with no Rigidbody on Ball and let it hang for three seconds, stop, add the Rigidbody, then press Play again and let the ball roll to the far wall.

page.title: The Rigidbody fields
page.text: Mass is how heavy the ball is to the physics engine. Use Gravity pulls the ball down. Linear Damping is a brake on moving; at 0 there is none. There are no fields called Drag or Angular Drag in this version.

Before you added the Rigidbody, the ball stayed where it was. After you added it, the ball fell onto the ramp, rolled down it, crossed the floor and came to rest against Wall_North. It went wrong if the ball falls through the ramp (the Sphere Collider is switched off), if it never moves (the Rigidbody is missing, or you added Rigidbody 2D) or if it rolls off to the side (check the Ramp Rotation is 20, 0, 0).

page.alt: The red-orange Ball rolling down the yellow Ramp in the lit Arena during Play.
page.caption: Halfway down the ramp, about two seconds after pressing Play.
page.shows: The Game view during Play with the ball halfway down the ramp, and the Hierarchy visible with Ramp and Ball.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The ball never moves when you press Play: it has no Rigidbody. Add Component, type Rigidbody and pick Rigidbody, not Rigidbody 2D.

The ball falls through the ramp or floor: its Sphere Collider is unticked, or the Ramp’s Box Collider is unticked. Tick them.

The ball misses the ramp: check the Ball Position is 0, 6, -7 and the Ramp Position is 0, 2, -4.
Test what a Rigidbody and a collider each do
You now have a working scene, so you will break it on purpose. Switching one thing off at a time is the fastest way to learn which component does which job, and the same trick finds bugs later.

items.text: Make sure Play is off. Click **Ball** in the **Hierarchy**.
In the **Rigidbody** section, untick **Use Gravity**. Click **Play**. The ball hangs in the air. Click **Play** to stop, then tick **Use Gravity** again.

Untick the checkbox at the left of the **Sphere Collider** heading. Click **Play**. The ball falls straight through the ramp and the floor and keeps going. Click **Play** to stop, then tick the box again.

shot.alt: Ball Inspector with the Sphere Collider heading unticked and the Rigidbody section below it.
shot.caption: The box at the left of the Sphere Collider heading, unticked.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Ball with the Sphere Collider checkbox unticked and the Rigidbody section below it. Outline the Sphere Collider checkbox.

items.text: Click **Ball** and choose **Edit > Duplicate**. The copy is called Ball (1) and is selected. Choose **Edit > Rename**, type Ball_Heavy and press Enter.
Set the **Position** of Ball_Heavy to 2, 6, -7 and its **Mass** to 10.
Click **Ball** and set its **Position** to -2, 6, -7.
Click **Play** and watch both balls. They land and roll together, side by side. Click **Play** to stop.

shot.alt: Two balls, Ball and Ball_Heavy, rolling down the ramp side by side at the same height.
shot.caption: Mass 1 and Mass 10, side by side all the way down.
shot.shows: The Game view during Play with Ball and Ball_Heavy side by side on the ramp at the same height. Outline both balls.

items.text: Click **Play** again. While it runs, click **Ball** and change **Mass** to 50.
Click **Play** to stop, then click **Ball**. **Mass** reads 1 again, because changes made during Play are thrown away.
Click **Ball_Heavy** and choose **Edit > Delete**.
Click **Ball** and set its **Position** back to 0, 6, -7.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: What you learned
page.text: Without gravity the Rigidbody has no reason to move. Without the collider, the Rigidbody still falls, but nothing is solid enough to stop it. A heavier ball keeps up with a light one because gravity pulls harder on it and it is harder to move by the same amount.

The Hierarchy lists Floor, four walls, Ramp, Ball and the camera and light, but no Ball_Heavy. Ball has Mass 1, Use Gravity ticked and Sphere Collider ticked, at Position 0, 6, -7. Pressing Play shows the ball roll down the ramp again. It went wrong if the ball falls through things (a collider is still unticked) or if Mass is not 1.

page.alt: Ball Inspector: Sphere Collider on, Rigidbody Mass 1, Use Gravity ticked; Hierarchy has no Ball_Heavy.
page.caption: Two of the tests: the collider switched off, then the light and heavy balls together.
page.shows: The Inspector for Ball showing Sphere Collider ticked and Rigidbody with Mass 1 and Use Gravity ticked, with the Hierarchy at left.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Mass is not 1 after Play: a change made during Play should reset when you stop. With Play off, select Ball rather than Ball_Heavy and set Mass to 1.

The balls do not land together: check both Positions have Y of 6 and Z of -7.

Edit > Delete is grayed out: click the object’s name in the Hierarchy first.

page.text: Challenges
These two challenges have no steps, because working things out yourself is how the components stick. Save the Arena first. Keep Play off while you change things.

Challenge: a bouncy ball. Add a second sphere named Ball_Bouncy at Position 6, 6, 4, with the M_Ball material and a Rigidbody. Make it bounce, so that when you press Play it falls onto the floor and bounces at least three times, each bounce lower than the last, before settling. The ramp does not reach that spot, so only the floor is in its way.

page.title: Hint
page.text: A bounce comes from a physics material on the ball’s collider. Make one with Assets > Create > Physics Material, name it PM_Bouncy, raise its Bounciness to 0.8 and set its Bounce Combine to Maximum. Drag it onto the Material box of the Sphere Collider, which reads None (Physics Material). Bounce Combine matters because the floor has no physics material: left on Average, the ball’s 0.8 is averaged with the floor’s 0 and it bounces only once.

Optional challenge: a lamp in the arena. Turn the arena into a dim room with one lamp. Lower the Directional Light Intensity to 0.4. Add a Point Light named Lamp (GameObject > Light > Point Light) at Position 0, 4, 3 with a warm yellow color. The floor and the ramp’s low end should glow near the lamp and the corners of the arena should look darker. Press Play and check the ball still rolls the same way.

page.title: Hint
page.text: A Point Light shines in all directions from one spot, and its Light component has the same Emission section as the Directional Light, with a Light Appearance setting for its color. A new Point Light has an Intensity of 1, which is too weak to see here: raise **Intensity** to about 30. Range only sets how far the light can reach, and the 10 it starts with is enough.

Your Ball_Bouncy bounces several times, each lower than the last. If you tried the optional challenge, your Lamp makes a bright patch near the middle of the floor while the floor far from it keeps its own color. The main Ball still rolls down the ramp. It went wrong if Ball_Bouncy does not bounce (the physics material is not on its Sphere Collider) or if nothing glows (Lamp Intensity is too low: try 30).

page.alt: Ball_Bouncy mid-bounce in a dimmed Arena with a warm patch of light on the floor.
page.caption: Ball_Bouncy with Bounciness 0.8 and Bounce Combine set to Maximum.
page.shows: The Game view during Play with Ball_Bouncy mid-bounce above the floor and the Lamp glow visible on the floor, and the Inspector showing the Sphere Collider Material box with PM_Bouncy.

page.text: Wrap-up

You can now add, switch off and read components in the Inspector, make a material and set its color and a light’s color, and make a ball fall and roll with a Rigidbody and colliders. Test yourself. Components: which two components give a Cube its looks and its solidity? Color: which box sets a material’s color, and what changes if you recolor the light? Physics: what happens to a Rigidbody ball with no collider, and what happens to a change you make during Play? Next time you write your first script, with variables, Start and Update, to spin an object, and you learn to read an error in the Console.

facilitation.announcement: This week your Courtyard shapes start to behave. Students make a new project called OrbCollector, build an Arena, color it with materials and a tinted light, and drop a ball onto a ramp with a Rigidbody. The one thing to get right: Rigidbody and colliders do different jobs, and changes made during Play are lost when Play stops. Please make fixes with Play off. Your first forum post is due by Thursday. Replies, the self-check quiz and the Weekly builds work are due by Sunday night. If the ball falls through the floor or never moves, open the Stuck? list on the page before you post.
watchFor: Students edit values during Play and then think the Inspector ‘forgot’ them. Ask them to stop Play, repeat the change and save, and point them to the Play-warning in the page.
The ball never moves because they added Rigidbody 2D instead of Rigidbody. Ask them to open the Ball Inspector and check the heading reads Rigidbody.
The ball falls through the floor because a collider was unticked in the tests and never re-ticked. Ask for a screenshot of the Inspector.
Students look for a color field called Albedo or Color on a material. Tell them it is the color box beside Base Map under Surface Inputs.
Students type only one Position number, so objects land in odd places. Remind them a new object does not start at 0, 0, 0 and to type all three numbers.
Submitted recordings show the Editor but no Play, or a stopped game. Ask them to record pressing Play and the ball rolling.
feedback: Your Arena matches the numbers, and the walls meet cleanly at the corners. Good care with the Transform values.
Your recording shows the ball falling, rolling and stopping, which proves the Rigidbody and colliders are working. Nice and clear.
You explained which component does which job in your own words, for example that the Mesh Renderer draws and the collider is solid. Keep naming components like this.
Your colors read well under the light. Try changing only the light color next time to see how much of the mood comes from the light.
Your forum reply built on a classmate’s idea with a specific test, such as unticking one component. That is the habit that finds bugs.
When something does not work, switch off one component at a time, as you did in the tests. Tell us which one changed the result.

l_bd8c2b118633.title: Your first C# script
l_bd8c2b118633.summary: Write a script with variables, Start and Update that spins an object, and learn to read Console errors; submit a recording and screenshot.
suggestedReadings: Hocking, J. (2022). Unity in Action (3rd ed.). Manning
keyIdeas: A script is a text file of C# instructions. When you attach it to a GameObject it becomes a component, like the Mesh Renderer and Rigidbody you met last week.

A variable is a named box that holds one value. A public variable also shows up in the Inspector, so you can change it there without touching the code. Once a component exists, the Inspector value wins over the starting value written in the code.
Start runs once when Play begins. Update runs once every frame. Multiplying by Time.deltaTime makes a speed mean the same thing on a slow computer and a fast one.
A Console error names the file, the line and column, a code and a short sentence. Read it, double-click it, fix the first error in the list first, then save and look again.

vocabulary.definition: A text file of C# instructions that, once attached to a GameObject, works as a component of your own.
A named box that holds one value, which a script can read and change.
A kind of variable that holds a number with a decimal point, such as 90f.
A kind of variable that holds either true or false.
A kind of variable that holds text written between quotation marks.
A block of a script that Unity runs once, when Play begins.
A block of a script that Unity runs once every frame while Play is on.
One picture drawn on your screen; a game draws many every second.
The window where Unity writes your Debug.Log messages, warnings and errors.
A mistake in your code that Unity finds when it turns the script into something it can run, and that stops Play from starting.
A line of code that writes a message to the Console so you can see what your script is doing.
The fraction of a second the last frame took, used to make speeds the same on fast and slow computers.

study.overview: This week you wrote your first script and made a cube turn with it. You can now create a script, attach it to a GameObject, change its variables to change what it does, and read a Console error to find and fix the line it points to. You will use all three habits every week from here on.

points.heading: A script becomes a component when you attach it
points.explanation: A script is a text file of C# instructions. When you attach it to a GameObject, it becomes a component, just like the Mesh Renderer and Rigidbody you met last week. The class inside the file takes the name you typed when you created it, and Unity matches the class to the file name. So type the name straight away, with the right capital letters. In your project you made Spinner with Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script and dragged it onto Pickup_Test. If the Inspector shows no Spinner (Script) section, the script is not attached: drag it again or use Add Component. If you see the message about no MonoBehaviour scripts, the file name and class name differ, so delete the script and create it again as Spinner.

points.heading: Variables are dials, and the Inspector value wins
points.explanation: A variable is a named box that holds one value. A public variable also shows in the Inspector, so you can change it without touching the code. Spinner has three: `public float speed = 90f;` (a number), `public bool isSpinning = true;` (true or false) and `public string message` (text). The number in the code is only the starting value. Once the component exists, the Inspector keeps its own copy, and that copy wins. For example, if you change the code to 45f but the Inspector still reads 180, the cube still spins at 180. Use the three-dot menu on the component and choose Reset to bring back the code’s value. Because each cube has its own copy, Pickup_Test can run at Speed 120 while Pickup_Test_B, a duplicate with the same script, runs at Speed 30. Changes you make during Play are thrown away when you stop.

points.heading: Start runs once, Update runs every frame
points.explanation: `Start` runs once when Play begins. In Spinner it writes Spinner started on Pickup_Test to the Console a single time. `Update` runs once per frame, so it holds the code for things that keep happening. `transform.Rotate(0f, speed * Time.deltaTime, 0f);` turns the cube a little each frame. Time.deltaTime is the fraction of a second the last frame took. Speed times that fraction means 90 turns the cube 90 degrees every second, on a slow computer or a fast one. Without it, a fast computer would spin the cube faster. Putting the Rotate line inside `if (isSpinning)` lets the tick box stop it.

points.heading: Read a Console error, then fix the first one first
points.explanation: A Console error gives you four things: the file, the line and column in brackets, a code, and a short sentence. For example, Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs(17,45): error CS1002: ; expected means the file Spinner.cs, line 17, column 45, code CS1002, and a missing semicolon. Double-click the message to jump to that line. If the line looks fine, check the line above it. Compiler errors stop Play from starting. C# is case sensitive: `Time.deltatime` gives CS0117 because Time has no such name, and `Transform.Rotate` with a capital T gives CS0120 because Rotate needs one particular object. Fix the first error in the list, save, click back into Unity and look again, because one mistake often causes the rest. Click Clear if an old message stays. Lines from older tutorials such as `Input.GetKey` throw an error in this version, so do not copy them.

page.text: Last week you built an Arena and watched physics move a ball. Nothing in it follows your own instructions yet. This week that changes. You write your first script, a short text file in the language C#, and attach it to a cube so it spins. You change its variables to speed it up, slow it down and stop it. Then you break the script on purpose, read the error the Console gives you, and fix the line it points to. By Sunday you will have a spinning cube in your OrbCollector project, a screenshot and a recording of it, and the habit of reading errors before panicking.

Create the Spinner script and attach it to a cube
A script is how you tell an object what to do in your own words, so you start with a short video on what one is, then make an empty script and put it on an object.

page.alt: A script file with the class line, Start, Update and three variables marked, then a Console error with its file, line, column and code marked.
page.shows: The instructor’s voice over the Unity Editor. First the empty script template open in Visual Studio Code with the words class, Start and Update highlighted in turn. Then the same file with the three variables added, with each type word (float, bool, string) circled as it is mentioned. Last the Console tab with a red error message, the file name, the two numbers in brackets and the code each outlined as they are named.
page.transcript:
Hello. Last week you used components that Unity gives you: a Mesh Renderer to draw a cube, a Rigidbody to let physics move it. This week you make a component of your own. It is called a script.

A script is a text file of instructions, written in a language called C#, pronounced C sharp. You attach it to a GameObject, and from then on it is a component like any other. Unity reads it and does what it says.

Look at the file Unity gives you when you create one. There is a line that starts with the word class. That is the name of your script, and it must match the file name exactly, capital letters included. Inside you find two blocks of instructions. The first is called Start. Unity runs it once for each enabled script instance, before its first Update. On your active cube, this happens when Play begins. The second is called Update. Unity runs it again and again, once for every frame. A frame is one picture on your screen. A game that draws sixty frames a second runs Update sixty times a second.

Now variables. A variable is a named box that holds one value. You say what kind of value it holds, then its name, then what it starts as. A float holds a number that can include a fractional part, such as 90 or 45.5. A bool holds true or false. A string holds text in quotation marks. If you write the word public in front, the box shows up in the Inspector, and you can change it there without touching the code.

To spin a cube we use one line in Update. Rotate turns the object by an amount each frame. We multiply the speed by Time.deltaTime, which is the time the last frame took, a tiny fraction of a second. That makes the speed mean degrees per second, whether your computer draws thirty frames or one hundred and twenty.

Last, errors. You will make mistakes this week, on purpose and by accident. Everyone does, every day. When you make one, Unity writes a message in the Console, the tab at the bottom. The message tells you the file, then two numbers in brackets: the line and the column. Then a code, and a short sentence. Read that sentence, double-click the message, and Unity takes you to the line. Fix the first error in the list first, because one mistake often causes the others.

Now open Unity, and let’s make your cube spin.

page.text: You need an object to put the script on. Later in the course your pickups will spin, so you make a stand-in cube now. It borrows the yellow material from last week.

page.text: Why the name matters: the class inside the file takes the name you typed when you created it. Unity matches that class to the file name, so if you rename the file later, the script stops working.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The message No MonoBehaviour scripts in the file, or their names do not match the file name. The file name and the class name differ, often by a capital letter. Delete the script in the Project window, then create it again as Spinner.

You cannot find the cube in the Game view. Check that its Position reads -5, 1, 5: it belongs near the back left corner of the Arena.

The cube is white, not yellow. M_Ramp did not land on it. Drag M_Ramp from the Materials folder onto Pickup_Test in the Hierarchy.
Write the code that spins the cube
Right now Spinner is an empty shell, so you fill it with a few lines that tell the cube to turn, and you learn what each line does.

items.text: In the **Project** window, double-click the Spinner script. Visual Studio Code opens with the file.
You will see a short file with a class line and two blocks, Start and Update, each with a comment above it. Click anywhere in the file.
Select everything: press Ctrl+A on Windows or Cmd+A on a Mac. Press Delete.
Type the file shown below, exactly as written. Indent with the Tab key. Capital letters, brackets and semicolons all matter.

page.caption: Spinner.cs

items: `using UnityEngine;` lets the file use Unity’s own words, such as Debug and Time. Leave it as the first line.
`public class Spinner : MonoBehaviour` names the script Spinner and says it can be attached to a GameObject as a component. The braces `{ }` mark where it begins and ends.

`public float speed = 90f;` makes a variable. A float is a number with a decimal point, the name is speed, and it starts at 90. The f marks it as a float. Because it is public, it shows in the Inspector.
`public bool isSpinning = true;` makes a bool, a variable that is either true or false.
`public string message = "Spinner started on ";` makes a string, a variable that holds text between quotation marks.
`void Start()` defines instructions Unity runs once for each enabled script instance, before its first Update.
`Debug.Log(message + gameObject.name);` writes a line to the Console. The plus joins the message to the name of the object the script is on. The semicolon ends the instruction.
`void Update()` is a block Unity runs once per frame, and a frame is one picture on your screen.
`if (isSpinning)` means: only run the lines inside the braces when isSpinning is true.

`transform.Rotate(0f, speed * Time.deltaTime, 0f);` turns this object by the three numbers given, as degrees around its x, y and z axes. Only the middle number, around the vertical axis, is not zero. `Time.deltaTime` is the fraction of a second the last frame took. Speed times that fraction is the turn for one frame, so 90 means 90 degrees every second.

items.text: Save the file: press Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac.
Click back into the Unity Editor. A small spinning icon at the bottom right shows Unity is compiling, which means turning your text into something the computer can run. Wait until it stops.
Click the **Console** tab at the bottom of the Editor. If you cannot see it, choose **Window > General > Console**.

page.text:

Change variables to change behavior
Variables are the dials of your script, so you turn them to see how one script can behave in many ways without a single new line of code.

items.text: Click Pickup_Test in the **Hierarchy**. In the **Spinner (Script)** section of the **Inspector** you see **Speed** 90, **Is Spinning** ticked and **Message**. Unity turns the names speed, isSpinning and message into these labels.

While the game runs, set **Speed** to 360. The cube now turns once a second.
Set **Speed** to -90. It turns the other way.
Untick **Is Spinning**. The cube stops. Tick it again.

page.text: Next you find out which value wins when the code and the Inspector disagree. The number in the code is only the starting value, the one Unity uses when the script is first attached. After that, the Inspector keeps its own copy.

items.text: Double-click Spinner in the **Project** window. In the file, change `public float speed = 90f;` to `public float speed = 45f;`.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac, then click back into Unity and wait for compiling to finish.
Click Pickup_Test. **Speed** still reads 180. The Inspector value wins.
In the **Spinner (Script)** heading, click the three-dot menu at the right and choose **Reset**. **Speed** becomes 45, the value in the code.
Set **Speed** to 120.
Click Pickup_Test in the **Hierarchy** and choose **Edit > Duplicate**. The copy is called Pickup_Test (1). Choose **Edit > Rename**, type Pickup_Test_B and press Enter.
Set the **Position** of Pickup_Test_B to -8, 1, 5 and its **Speed** to 30.
Click **Play**. The two cubes turn at different speeds, from one script. Stop Play.

shot.alt: Two cubes in the Scene view, Pickup_Test_B Inspector Speed 30
shot.caption: Pickup_Test and Pickup_Test_B near the back left corner, both in the Hierarchy.
shot.shows: The Scene view with Pickup_Test and Pickup_Test_B side by side, the Hierarchy listing both, and the Inspector showing Speed 30 for Pickup_Test_B.

page.text: Pickup_Test has Speed 120 and Pickup_Test_B has Speed 30, and both cubes use the same Spinner script. When you press Play they turn at different speeds. If both turn at the same speed, check the Speed of each cube in the Inspector.

Reading for this part: Hocking, J. (2022). Unity in Action (3rd ed.). Manning. Find the chapter where Hocking writes a first script that makes a cube rotate, using the book’s contents page. Read it to see how he attaches a script to an object and how he uses Update, and compare it with what you did. Hocking’s movement code uses the old Input class, for example Input.GetAxis. In this version of Unity that throws an error, so do not copy those lines. You will read keys the new way next week.
Break the script and fix it from the Console
You will make errors for the rest of your life as a programmer, so you break Spinner on purpose in three small ways to learn what each message looks like and how to follow it back to the line.

The Console shows three kinds of message. A plain message, like your Debug.Log line, has an information icon. A warning has a triangle icon and does not stop the game. An error has an error icon. Compiler errors stop Play from starting. Runtime errors appear while the game runs; Play may continue, but the affected instructions fail. The compiler errors you will create here follow this pattern. Here is an example: Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs(17,45): error CS1002: ; expected. The first part, Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs, is the file. The numbers in brackets mean line 17, column 45. CS1002 is the error code, handy for searching the web. The rest is the problem in plain words: a semicolon was expected. If the line looks fine, look at the line above it: the real mistake is sometimes there.
Break 1: a missing semicolon

items.text: In Visual Studio Code, in Spinner.cs, find the line `Debug.Log(message + gameObject.name);`.
Delete the semicolon at the end of that line.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac, then click back into Unity.
Click the **Console** tab. A new message appears with an error icon.

Read the message. Find the file name, the line and column in brackets, the code and the sentence. With the file typed exactly as given, it reads CS1002 and ; expected, at line 17, column 45. Your numbers may differ a little if your spacing differs.

shot.alt: Console error Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs(17,45): error CS1002: ; expected
shot.caption: The missing semicolon: file, line 17, column 45, code CS1002, and the sentence.
shot.shows: The Console with one error selected, its text fully visible: Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs(17,45): error CS1002: ; expected. Outline the file name, the numbers in brackets and the code.

items.text: Click **Play**. Play does not start, and the Console says All compiler errors have to be fixed before you can enter playmode!
Double-click the error message. Visual Studio Code opens with the cursor on that line.
Type the semicolon back, save, and click back into Unity. The error disappears. If an old message stays, click **Clear**.

page.text: Break 2: a misspelled name

items.text: In `transform.Rotate(0f, speed * Time.deltaTime, 0f);` change `Time.deltaTime` to `Time.deltatime`, with a small t. Save and click back into Unity.

In the **Console**, read the message. It reads Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs(25,47): error CS0117: ‘Time’ does not contain a definition for ‘deltatime’. It says exactly what is wrong: Time has no such name. C# is case sensitive, so deltatime and deltaTime are different names.

shot.alt: Console error CS0117: ‘Time’ does not contain a definition for ‘deltatime’
shot.caption: The misspelled name: line 25, column 47, code CS0117.
shot.shows: The Console with the CS0117 error selected and its full text visible. Outline deltatime in the message.

items.text: Double-click the message, fix the capital T, save, and click back into Unity. The error goes.

page.text: Break 3: a capital letter that changes the meaning

items.text: Change `transform.Rotate` to `Transform.Rotate`, with a capital T. Save and click back into Unity.

In the **Console**, read the message. Error CS0120 begins An object reference is required for the non-static field, method, or property. In plain words: Transform with a capital T is the general idea of a Transform, but Rotate needs one particular object to turn.

shot.alt: Console error CS0120: An object reference is required for the non-static field, method, or property
shot.caption: The capital T: line 25, column 13, code CS0120.
shot.shows: The Console with the CS0120 error selected and its text visible.

items.text: Change it back to `transform.Rotate`, with a small t. The small-t transform means the Transform component of the object this script is on.
Save, click back into Unity, and click **Play**. The cubes spin again. Stop Play.

page.title: An error you will meet from old tutorials
page.text: One error you may meet when you copy code from older tutorials is InvalidOperationException: You are trying to read Input using the UnityEngine.Input class, but you have switched active Input handling to Input System package in Player Settings. It appears when you press Play, not when you save. Your project reads input with the Input System package, so lines like Input.GetKey do not work here. Next week you read keys the right way.

The Console has no red messages, and Play starts and both cubes spin. You can describe an error by naming its file, line and column, code and sentence. If a red message stays after you fixed the line, click Clear. If it comes back, you did not save or fix the first error in the list.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The Console shows nothing after you broke the line. You did not save, or Unity has not finished compiling. Save the file, click back into the Unity window and wait for the spinning icon to stop.

Several errors appear at once. Fix the first one and save: one mistake often makes the rest.

The Console tab is missing. Choose Window > General > Console.
Capture a screenshot and a screen recording
From here on you will often need to show what is on your screen, for the forum and for getting help, so you learn to capture a screenshot and a recording on your own computer.
On Windows

items.text: For a screenshot, press the Windows key + Shift + S. The screen dims. Drag a rectangle around the part you want. The picture goes to the clipboard and a small notification appears.
Click the notification. Snipping Tool opens. Press Ctrl+S, choose a folder such as Pictures, name it console and save.
For a recording, press the Windows key + G to open Xbox Game Bar. Click the Unity window first so it is the active window.
Press the Windows key + Alt + R to start recording, and press it again to stop.
Open File Explorer and go to Videos > Captures. Your recording is there as an .mp4 file.

page.text: On a Mac

items.text: For a screenshot, press Shift+Command+4, then drag a rectangle around the part you want. The picture is saved to your Desktop as a .png file.
For a recording, press Shift+Command+5. A toolbar appears at the bottom of the screen.
Click **Record Selected Portion**, drag a rectangle around the Unity window, and click **Record**.
To stop, click the stop button in the menu bar at the top of the screen.
Your recording is saved to the Desktop as a .mov file.

page.text: Practice with your own work

items.text: Take a screenshot of the **Console** with the line Spinner started on Pickup_Test visible, and of the Inspector showing Spinner (Script).
Record about ten seconds: click **Play**, let both cubes turn, click **Play** to stop.
Open both files from where they were saved to check them. The picture should be readable and the recording should show the cubes turning.

page.text: You have a picture file you can open and read, and a recording that is under a minute and shows the cubes turning. If the recording is black or shows another window, record again with the Unity window active. If the picture is too small to read, drag a bigger rectangle.
Challenges: tumble and speed up
These challenges have no steps, because working out what a line does is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.
Challenge: make the cube tumble

Change Spinner so a cube turns around two axes at once. It keeps its Speed around its local y-axis and also turns around its local x-axis at a new speed that shows in the Inspector as Tumble Speed. These axes turn with the cube, so its local y-axis will tilt as it tumbles. Ticking off Is Spinning still stops both turns. Each cube has its own Tumble Speed, so Pickup_Test can be set to 0 to spin flat while Pickup_Test_B tumbles at 45.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Rotate takes three numbers: x, y and z. Your Speed line fills the middle one. Add a new public float for the first one, and give it the same treatment as speed. Keep the Rotate line inside the braces of the if, so Is Spinning controls it.
Optional challenge: a spin that speeds up

Make a cube that starts slow and winds up like a fan. Add two public floats, Acceleration and Max Speed. While Play is on, Speed grows by Acceleration degrees per second every second, and it never goes above Max Speed. Set Pickup_Test_B to Speed 30, Acceleration 60 and Max Speed 360: it should reach full speed after about five and a half seconds and stay there. When you stop Play, Speed goes back to 30. Later in the course, hazards in your Dodge game will speed up in the same way.

page.title: Hint
page.text: To add to a variable, write `speed += acceleration * Time.deltaTime;`. The += means: add this to what is already there. To stop it going too high, follow it with an if that checks whether speed is larger than maxSpeed and, if so, sets speed to maxSpeed. Put both in Update, before or after Rotate.

Press Play. For the first challenge, the cube turns around two axes and a tumbling cube stops when Is Spinning is off. For the optional one, the cube visibly speeds up and then holds steady. If nothing changes, check you saved Spinner.cs. After testing, stop Play and choose File > Save to save the cubes and their Inspector settings in your Arena scene. If there is a red message, read it and double-click it.

page.alt: Spinner (Script) with Tumble Speed 45 and a cube tumbling in the Scene view
page.caption: One result: Tumble Speed 45 on Pickup_Test_B and 0 on Pickup_Test. Tumble Speed shows in the Inspector under Speed.
page.shows: The Inspector of Pickup_Test_B showing Spinner (Script) with Speed, Is Spinning, Message and Tumble Speed (45), and the Scene view with the cube mid-tumble.

page.label: OrbCollector as it should stand at the end of this week: the Arena, the Scripts folder with Spinner, and the cubes Pickup_Test and Pickup_Test_B using it. Use it if your own project is stuck, then compare it with yours to find the difference.

page.text: Wrap-up

You can now create a script and attach it to a GameObject, declare variables and change them in the Inspector or in code, and read a Console error to fix the line it points to. Test yourself. First, what do you need to match when you name a script, and how do you attach it? Second, which value wins when the code says 90 and the Inspector says 180, and how do you reset it? Third, what four things does a Console error tell you? Next week you move the ball with keyboard input and forces in FixedUpdate, and make the camera follow it.

facilitation.announcement: Welcome to this week. You write your first script, a short C# file called Spinner, and attach it to a cube in your OrbCollector project so that it spins. You change its variables, then break it on purpose and learn to read the errors in the Console. The one thing to get right: the script’s file name and the class name inside it must match exactly, capital letters included, and when something goes red, read the first error and double-click it. Deadlines: your first forum post by Thursday; replies, the Weekly builds work and everything else by Sunday night. If you get stuck, post the exact Console text and a screenshot in the forum, and I will answer there.
watchFor: File name and class name do not match, shown as No MonoBehaviour scripts in the file, or their names do not match the file name. Ask for a screenshot of the Project window. The quickest fix is to delete the script and recreate it with the name typed right away.

Missing semicolons, brackets or capital letters when typing the code, and several errors at once. Remind students to fix the first error in the list, save, and look again, rather than fixing them all at once.
Forum posts that say only that it does not work. Ask for the exact Console message, its line and column, and the Inspector with Spinner (Script) showing.

Students who change values during Play and think they lost them, or who edit the number in the code and see no change. Point them to the changes-are-thrown-away idea from last week and to Reset on the component’s three-dot menu.

Code copied from web tutorials that uses Input.GetKey or Input.GetAxis, which throws InvalidOperationException in this version. Tell them it is expected, that input comes next week, and not to copy those lines.
Visual Studio Code not opening from Unity, or opening a different editor. Point to External Tools, External Script Editor in Edit > Preferences... on Windows, or Unity > Settings... on a Mac.
feedback: Your Console error is quoted in full and you found the line it points to. That is the skill this week. Keep doing that whenever something fails.
Your recording shows both cubes turning at different speeds, so I can see you used the Inspector values instead of editing the code each time. Nice.
The script works, but the screenshot does not show the Console or Inspector. Next time, drag the rectangle round the part that proves the result.
Your code ran, but a comment or name is hard to read. Short names like speed and isSpinning tell the reader what a variable is for. Keep that habit.
You asked a classmate a useful question and quoted the error text. Posts like that get answered fastest.
Your challenge result tumbles on two axes. Try one more change: set Tumble Speed to a negative number and describe what happens in the forum.
facilitation.atRisk: On Wednesday evening, message privately anyone who has no forum post yet, and anyone whose post says the script will not compile. Ask for a screenshot of the Console and of the Spinner (Script) section, and point them to the Stuck? list first. If a student still has no working Spinner on Friday, send them the checkpoint file and ask them to open it and compare.

l_27ca80e9c09a.title: Input and movement
l_27ca80e9c09a.summary: Move the ball with keyboard input and forces in FixedUpdate, and make the camera follow it; submit a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: Read the keys in Update and apply forces in FixedUpdate. Update runs once per frame. FixedUpdate runs on the physics clock, which is when a Rigidbody listens for pushes.
This project uses the Input System package only. The old `Input.GetKey` and `Input.GetAxis` throw an error when the game runs, so you read keys with `Keyboard.current` or an input action.
A direction in 3D is a Vector3. Normalizing it gives it a length of 1, so moving diagonally is not faster than moving straight.
A camera that follows a target works out its offset once in Start, then sets its position to the target’s position plus that offset in LateUpdate.

vocabulary.definition: The package this project uses to read keys, mouse and game controllers.
The keyboard that is connected right now, which you ask about keys such as aKey.isPressed.
A named input such as Move that the project connects to real keys and controllers.
One value that holds three numbers, x, y and z, used for positions and directions.
A direction rescaled to length 1, so diagonal movement is not faster than straight movement.
A push on a Rigidbody that changes its speed a little at a time.
The Rigidbody method that gives physics a push to apply.
A method that Unity runs once per physics step, which is where forces go.
A Rigidbody field that slows the ball a little at every step, like a brake.
A method that runs after all the Update methods in a frame, used for cameras that follow.
The gap between two positions, kept so the camera stays the same distance from the ball.

study.overview: You can now take control of the ball. You read the keyboard, turn what you read into a push that physics understands, and keep the camera a steady distance behind the ball. This page is the one to reread before next week, when you build on the same ball and the same two scripts.

points.heading: Read keys in Update, push in FixedUpdate
points.explanation: Update runs once per frame, so it is the place to ask which keys are held. FixedUpdate runs on the physics clock, which is when a Rigidbody listens for pushes, so `rb.AddForce(moveInput * speed);` goes there. Update saves the direction in a variable such as `moveInput`, and FixedUpdate uses it. Because `AddForce` adds a little speed at every step, the ball speeds up while you hold a key and coasts when you let go. Linear Damping removes a little speed at every step: with it at 1 the ball stops soon after you release the keys, and at 0 it keeps rolling. If a jump press can fall between two physics steps, store it in a bool in Update and use it in FixedUpdate.

points.heading: Read input with the Input System, not the old Input class
points.explanation: This project uses the Input System package only. `Input.GetKey` and `Input.GetAxis` compile, but the game stops with an InvalidOperationException when it runs. Add `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` and read a key with `Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed`. Check that `Keyboard.current` is not null first, because it is empty when no keyboard is connected. Or read the project’s Move action: `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` once in Start, then `moveAction.ReadValue<Vector2>()` each frame. The name in quotes must match exactly. The action’s y goes into the z slot of a Vector3, because the ball moves along the floor: `new Vector3(moveInput.x, 0f, moveInput.y)`.

points.heading: Directions are Vector3s, and normalizing keeps diagonals fair
points.explanation: A Vector3 holds three numbers, x, y and z. Holding W and D together would give (1, 0, 1), which is longer than (1, 0, 0), so the ball would move faster on the diagonal. `.normalized` rescales a direction to length 1. That is why W and D together print (0.71, 0.00, 0.71) in the Console, and why the Move action already gives diagonals of length 1. Holding A and D together cancels to zero, so no push is applied.

points.heading: A follow camera stores a gap once and reapplies it
points.explanation: In Start, `offset = transform.position - target.position;` stores the gap between the camera and the Player, taken from where you placed the camera (0, 8, -10 in this build). In LateUpdate, `transform.position = target.position + offset;` puts the camera that same gap from the ball in every frame. LateUpdate runs after all the Update methods, so the ball has already moved. The script copies only the position, so the camera never turns and the view stays steady while the ball rolls. If the Target field is empty, you get an UnassignedReferenceException: drag Player onto Target. Test your understanding before you submit your Weekly builds item: change the camera’s starting position and predict where the camera will sit.

page.text: Last week you wrote a script that spun a cube all by itself. This week the player takes control. You will read the keyboard, push your ball with physics forces, and write a second script that keeps the camera behind the ball. Each piece is small, and each builds on skills you already have: variables, Start, Update and reading the Console. By Sunday night you will have a ball you can roll around the arena with the keys, a camera that follows it, and a short recording that shows it working.

This week builds on the OrbCollector project you already have, so you start by opening it and checking that your ball is ready to be moved.

Make the ball read the keyboard
Before a ball can move, your code has to know which keys are held, so you write a script that reads W, A, S and D and reports the direction it sees.
