Then a script with Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed highlighted. Then a Vector3 drawn as an arrow on the Scene view grid, then the Rigidbody component with Linear Damping circled, then a simple timeline with Update ticks and FixedUpdate ticks beneath it.
page.transcript:
Last week you wrote a script that turned a cube. The cube moved by itself. This week the player decides. Three ideas make that work.

First, input. This project uses Unity’s Input System package. The older Input class, with Input.GetAxis and Input.GetKey, still compiles, but it throws an error as soon as the game runs. If a tutorial online uses it, that is why it fails for you. Instead, you ask Keyboard.current about a key. Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed is true while A is held down. Later this week you will also read an input action called Move, which hands you a direction in one line.

Second, direction. A direction in 3D is three numbers: how far along x, y and z. Unity keeps three numbers together in one value called a Vector3. In this game, x is left and right, z is forward and back, and y is up. Pressing D gives x of one. Pressing W gives z of one. Both at once gives one and one, which is longer than one, so a ball would go faster on a diagonal. Calling normalized squashes any direction back to length one.

Third, force. Your ball has a Rigidbody, so physics moves it. You do not set its position. You push it with AddForce, and physics works out the speed, the bounce and the roll. A force changes speed bit by bit, so the ball speeds up while you push and coasts when you stop. Linear Damping, a field on the Rigidbody, is the brake that slows it down.

Where do you push? In FixedUpdate. Update runs once per frame, and a fast computer makes more frames. Physics does not work that way. It runs in steps of equal size, by default fifty a second, and FixedUpdate runs once per step. So the rule is: read the keys in Update, because you must not miss a key press, and apply the force in FixedUpdate, because that is when physics is listening. With its default force mode, `AddForce` already accounts for the physics step length. You do not multiply this force by `Time.deltaTime` again.

One more thing. Once the ball moves, the camera must follow it. You will do that in `LateUpdate`, which runs after the frame’s `Update` methods. The camera will follow the ball’s current displayed position.

Keep the Console open, and let’s build it.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the Scripts folder inside **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**.
The new script’s name is in edit mode. Type PlayerController and press Enter. The capital P and C matter, because the name must match the class name in the code.

shot.alt: Scripts folder containing Spinner and a new script being named PlayerController.
shot.shows: The Project window with the Scripts folder open, showing Spinner and a new script whose name box is in edit mode with PlayerController typed in. Windows or Mac.

items.text: Double-click PlayerController. Visual Studio Code opens with the file.
Click anywhere in the file. Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac) and press Delete.
Type the file shown below, exactly as written. Indent with the Tab key.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the small compiling spinner at the bottom right to finish.
In the **Hierarchy**, click Player. In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type PlayerController and press Enter.

shot.alt: Add Component search showing PlayerController as the result for the typed text PlayerController.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Player with the Add Component search box open and PlayerController typed in, the matching result listed. Outline the result.

items.text: In the **Player Controller (Script)** section, check that **Speed** reads 10.
Click **Play**. Click once inside the **Game** view so it receives your keys. Hold D, then release it. Hold W and D together, then release them.
Look at the **Console** tab. Click **Play** again to stop.

shot.alt: Console lines: Move input: (1.00, 0.00, 0.00) for D alone and Move input: (0.71, 0.00, 0.71) for W and D together.
shot.shows: The Console tab after the test. Outline the lines starting Move input, one with (1.00, 0.00, 0.00) and one with (0.71, 0.00, 0.71).

page.caption: PlayerController.cs

page.text: Here is what the new lines do. `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` lets your script use the Input System package. Without it, Unity does not know the word Keyboard. `private Vector3 moveInput;` is a variable like speed, but private means it does not show in the Inspector. A Vector3 is one value that holds three numbers, x, y and z.

`Keyboard keyboard = Keyboard.current;` copies the current keyboard into a short name. `if (keyboard == null)` guards against there being none, and `return;` ends the method early. `keyboard.aKey.isPressed` is true on every frame that A is held down. Each `if` line nudges x or z by one, so holding A and D together cancels to zero. `.normalized` rescales the direction to length 1. That is why W and D together print 0.71 and 0.71, not 1 and 1. The last line writes a message only when a key is held, so the Console does not fill with empty lines.

page.title: Why not Input.GetKey?
page.text: In the old Input class you would write Input.GetKey. In this project that class is switched off. It compiles, but the game stops with an InvalidOperationException when it runs. Using Keyboard.current avoids it.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Likely causes if the Console stays empty or shows an error:

Nothing prints when you press keys. You did not click inside the Game view first, or PlayerController is not on Player. Click Player and look for the Player Controller (Script) section.

error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘Keyboard’ could not be found. The line `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` is missing or mistyped at the top of the file.

InvalidOperationException: You are trying to read Input using the UnityEngine.Input class, but you have switched active Input handling to Input System package in Player Settings. A line in your file still uses Input.GetKey or Input.GetAxis. Replace it with the code above.

Add Component does not find PlayerController. The file name and the class name differ, or the Console shows a compile error. Fix the first error in the Console list, save and wait for the spinner.

In Play, holding D prints Move input: (1.00, 0.00, 0.00). Holding W and D together prints (0.71, 0.00, 0.71). Releasing everything prints nothing. It went wrong if every line shows (0.00, 0.00, 0.00), which means the key names in your code are wrong, or if you see a red error: read it as you did last week, starting with the first one.
Push the ball with a force in FixedUpdate
Now the direction you read becomes a real push, so the ball rolls the way physics rolls a ball: it speeds up while you push and coasts when you let go.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click Player. In the **Rigidbody** section of the **Inspector**, set **Linear Damping** to 1. This slows the ball when you let go of the keys. In the same Rigidbody section, set **Interpolate** to **Interpolate**. This smooths the ball’s displayed movement between physics steps.

shot.alt: Rigidbody with Mass 1, Linear Damping 1, Angular Damping 0.05, Use Gravity ticked.
shot.shows: The Rigidbody section of the Inspector for Player. Outline Linear Damping with the value 1, and show Mass 1, Angular Damping 0.05 and Use Gravity ticked.

items.text: In the **Project** window, double-click PlayerController to open it in Visual Studio Code.
Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
Click **Play**. Click once inside the **Game** view. Hold W, then D, then S, then A, and let go between each one.

While the game is running, click Player and set **Speed** to 25 in the **Player Controller (Script)** section. Click inside the **Game** view and push the ball again. Then set **Speed** to 3, click inside the **Game** view again and push again. If the ball rolls off the edge of the Arena, click **Play** to stop and start again.

shot.alt: Player Controller (Script) with Speed 25 while the ball rolls across the Game view.
shot.shows: The Game view in Play mode beside the Inspector. Outline the Speed field showing 25 in the Player Controller (Script) section, and the ball mid-roll in the Game view.

items.text: Click **Play** to stop. Look at **Speed**: it is back at 10, because changes made during Play are thrown away.
With Play off, set **Linear Damping** to 0, click **Play**, click inside the **Game** view, hold D briefly and let go. Watch the ball keep rolling. Stop Play and set **Linear Damping** back to 1.

page.caption: PlayerController.cs

page.text: Three things are new. `private Rigidbody rb;` is a variable that holds the ball’s Rigidbody. `GetComponent<Rigidbody>()` asks the object this script is on for its Rigidbody. You do it once in `Start` and keep the answer in `rb`, so you do not search again at every step.

`void FixedUpdate()` is a method like Update, but Unity runs it once per physics step instead of once per frame. `moveInput * speed` multiplies each of the three numbers by speed, so a direction of length 1 becomes a push of length 10. `rb.AddForce(...)` hands that push to physics, which adds a little to the ball’s speed at every step while the push lasts. There is no extra `Time.deltaTime` multiplier because `AddForce` in its default force mode already uses the physics step length to calculate the change in velocity. The test line with Debug.Log is gone, since it has done its job.

page.alt: The ball speeds up while D is held and then slows to a stop after the key is released, with Linear Damping 1 shown in the Inspector.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode with the Player ball on the Arena floor. Hold D for about two seconds so the ball picks up speed, then release it and let the ball slow down and stop. Keep the Inspector for Player visible beside it with Linear Damping 1 readable. Windows or Mac.

page.title: Why the ball coasts
page.text: A force changes speed a little at every step. Linear Damping removes a little speed at every step. With damping 1 the two balance out at a top speed near 10, and the ball slows to a stop soon after you let go. With Linear Damping 0, this source of slowing is removed. The ball usually travels farther after you release the keys, but Angular Damping and contact friction can still affect its motion.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Likely causes if the ball does not behave:

The ball does not move and the Console shows NullReferenceException in FixedUpdate. `rb` was never filled in: the `Start` method is missing, or Player has no Rigidbody. Check the file against the code above and the Inspector for a Rigidbody section.

error CS0103: The name ‘rb’ does not exist in the current context. The line `private Rigidbody rb;` is missing or misspelled. Add it under `private Vector3 moveInput;`.

The ball does not move but there is no error. Click once inside the Game view, then check that Speed is not 0 in the Player Controller (Script) section. The Inspector value wins over the value in the code.

The ball is hard to stop. Check that Linear Damping is 1 on Player. The field is named Linear Damping in this version, and there is no field called Drag.

page.alt: Player ball away from the center of the Arena in Play mode, Speed 10 in the Inspector.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode with the ball rolled away from the center of the floor, and the Player Controller (Script) section of the Inspector beside it with Speed 10. Windows or Mac.

page.text: You should see the ball speed up while a key is held and slow down soon after you let go. Speed 25 makes it quick and twitchy, and Speed 3 makes it sluggish. It went wrong if the ball jumps from stopped to full speed at once (the code is setting speed, not adding force) or if nothing happens at all: use the Stuck? list above.
Read the Move action instead

Your keyboard code works, but it lists every key by hand, so you now swap it for the project’s own Move input action, which gives you the same direction in one line and keeps working when you add other controls.

An input action is a named input, such as Move or Jump, that the project’s Input System asset connects to real keys. Your project already has one. The InputSystem_Actions asset in the Assets folder has a Player map with Move, Look, Attack, Interact, Crouch, Jump, Previous, Next and Sprint. Move gives you a Vector2, which is one value holding two numbers: x for left and right, y for forward and back. The W, A, S and D keys are already connected to it, and diagonals are already length 1.

items.text: Double-click PlayerController in the **Project** window to open it in Visual Studio Code.
Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
In the **Hierarchy**, click Player and check that **Speed** in the **Player Controller (Script)** section still reads 10.

shot.alt: Player Controller (Script) with Speed 10.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Player with the Player Controller (Script) section open. Outline Speed with the value 10. Windows or Mac.

items.text: Click **Play**. Click once inside the **Game** view. Hold W, A, S and D one after another, then W and D together.
Click **Play** to stop.

page.caption: PlayerController.cs

page.text: `private InputAction moveAction;` is a variable that holds one input action. `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` looks the action up by its name, once, in `Start`. The name in quotes must match exactly, capital M included. `moveAction.ReadValue<Vector2>()` asks for its current value as a Vector2, so you get (0, 0) when nothing is held and a direction when keys are down. In `FixedUpdate`, `new Vector3(moveInput.x, 0f, moveInput.y)` puts the action’s y into the z slot, because the ball moves along the floor. The rest is the same push as before.

page.title: Why switch?
page.text: The keyboard version taught you how a key becomes a number. The action version is shorter, and the connection between keys and Move lives in the project’s Input System asset instead of in your code. Later in the course, a jump or a menu key is one more `FindAction` away.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Likely causes if the ball does not move or the Console shows an error:

NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object, pointing at the `ReadValue` line. `FindAction` found nothing, so check that the name in quotes is exactly Move.

error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘InputAction’ could not be found. The line `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` is missing at the top of the file.

The ball does not move and there is no error. Click once inside the Game view first, then check that Speed is not 0 in the Inspector.

page.alt: Player ball mid-roll in Play mode with an empty Console.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode with the ball mid-roll across the floor, and the Console tab below it empty. Windows or Mac.

page.text: You should see the ball roll exactly as before, with an empty Console. It went wrong if the Console shows a red error as soon as you click Play. Read the first one, double-click it and check the line it points to.
Make the camera follow the ball
At the moment the ball rolls out of sight, so you write a second script that keeps the camera at the same distance from the ball all the time.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the Scripts folder inside **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type CameraFollow and press Enter.
Double-click CameraFollow to open it. Select everything, press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written. Save it and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
In the **Hierarchy**, click Main Camera.
In the **Transform** section of the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 8, -10, **Rotation** to 37, 0, 0 and **Scale** to 1, 1, 1.

shot.alt: Main Camera Transform: Position 0, 8, -10, Rotation 37, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Main Camera. Outline Position 0, 8, -10, Rotation 37, 0, 0 and Scale 1, 1, 1 in the Transform section. Windows or Mac.

items.text: Click **Add Component**, type CameraFollow and press Enter.
In the **Hierarchy**, drag Player onto the **Target** field in the **Camera Follow (Script)** section of the **Inspector**.

shot.alt: Camera Follow (Script) with Target set to Player.
shot.shows: The Camera Follow (Script) section of the Inspector with Target showing Player after the drag. Outline the Target field. Windows or Mac.

items.text: Click **Play**. Click once inside the **Game** view and roll the ball around the Arena.
Click **Play** to stop. With Play off, set the Main Camera **Position** to 0, 5, -6 and click **Play** again. The camera follows from closer. Stop Play and set **Position** back to 0, 8, -10.

page.caption: CameraFollow.cs

page.text: `public Transform target;` is a variable that holds the position, rotation and scale of another object. Because it is public, it shows in the Inspector as **Target**, and you fill it by dragging Player onto it. `transform` with a small t is the Transform of the object this script is on, which is the camera. An offset is the gap between two positions. `transform.position - target.position` subtracts one Vector3 from another, which gives the gap, and you keep it in `offset`. `LateUpdate` adds that gap to the target’s position every frame, so the camera sits the same distance away wherever the ball goes. The camera never turns, so the ball can roll without the view spinning.

page.title: Why a script, and why LateUpdate
page.text: You could make the camera a child of the ball, but then it would roll and spin with it. A script that copies only the position keeps the view steady. `LateUpdate` runs after the frame’s `Update` methods. This lets the camera follow a target after movement performed in `Update`. The ball moves on the physics clock; its Rigidbody’s **Interpolate** setting smooths its displayed position between physics steps.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Likely causes if the camera does not follow:

UnassignedReferenceException: The variable target of CameraFollow has not been assigned. Target is empty, so drag Player from the Hierarchy onto the Target field.

The camera does not move and there is no error. CameraFollow is on the wrong object. Click Main Camera and look for the Camera Follow (Script) section.

The ball is out of view when you press Play. Check the Main Camera Position and Rotation from step 5, and that Player is at 0, 0.5, 0 when Play begins.

Add Component does not find CameraFollow. The file name and the class name differ, or the Console shows a compile error. Fix the first error in the list, save and wait.

page.alt: The camera glides after the ball as it rolls across the Arena, keeping it near the middle of the Game view.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode, full width. Roll the ball forward, left, back and right so it crosses most of the Arena. Show that the ball stays near the middle of the view while the floor and walls slide past. Windows or Mac.

page.text: You should see the ball stay in the same place in the Game view while the Arena moves past it. It went wrong if the camera stays still while the ball leaves the view, or if a red error appears when you press Play. Use the Stuck? list above.
Test the finished build
Before you record anything, you run through the whole build once, so that what you show is a version you know works.

items.text: Make sure Play is off. Choose **File > Save** to save the scene.
Click **Play**. Click once inside the **Game** view.
Roll the ball forward, back, left and right.
Roll it diagonally with W and D together. It should be no faster than straight.
Let go of every key and check that the ball coasts to a stop.
Look at the **Console**. There should be no red messages.

shot.alt: Game view with the ball in the Arena and an empty Console.
shot.shows: The Editor in Play mode with the Game view showing the ball and Arena and the Console tab open and empty. Windows or Mac.

items.text: Click **Play** to stop.

page.label: OrbCollector-week-checkpoint.zip
page.shows: The OrbCollector project as it should stand at the end of this week: PlayerController using the Move action, CameraFollow on the Main Camera with Player as its target, and Player with Linear Damping 1.

page.text: Use the checkpoint file only if your own project does not work and you cannot find why. Unzip it (Extract All on Windows, double-click on a Mac) and open the unzipped folder from the Projects screen in Unity Hub. When this part checks out, you are ready for your Weekly builds item.

You should see a ball that rolls in every direction, coasts to a stop, and stays near the middle of the view, with no red messages in the Console. It went wrong if a red message appears or the camera lags or jumps: go back to the Stuck? list in the part that covers it.
Challenges
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: add a jump. Change PlayerController so pressing Space gives the ball one upward push each time you press it. The push shows in the Inspector as **Jump Force** with a starting value of 5. Rolling still works. For now the ball may jump again while it is already in the air, and that is fine. Test it in your head: with Jump Force 5 and a Mass of 1, one press launches the ball upward at about 5 units per second, so it rises roughly one unit and falls back. Holding Space down does not keep launching it, because only the frame of the press counts.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Space is a key, so you can read it with `Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame`, which is true only on the frame the key goes down. A frame can pass between two physics steps, so a press could be missed if you tested it in FixedUpdate. Declare `private bool jumpRequested;` alongside your other variables. In `Update`, set it to true only when a press occurs: `if (Keyboard.current != null && Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame) { jumpRequested = true; }`. Leave it unchanged on frames without a press, so the request survives until `FixedUpdate` consumes it. Then, in FixedUpdate, jump if the bool is true and set it back to false. Use `rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);`. An impulse is a push all at once, so it suits a single jump. Check `Keyboard.current` is not null first.

Optional challenge: cap the top speed. Add a **Max Speed** field with a starting value of 8. Whatever the keys do, the ball’s flat speed, along x and z, never goes above Max Speed, while falling and jumping are not slowed. Test it in your head: set Max Speed to 4 and hold W. The ball speeds up, reaches 4 and stays there. Let go, and it still coasts to a stop. If you did the jump challenge, jumping still works.

page.title: Hint
page.text:
`rb.linearVelocity` is the ball’s velocity vector. Its flat speed is the length of its x and z parts. For this challenge, replace the horizontal `rb.AddForce(direction * speed);` line with the following lines, keeping each inside `FixedUpdate`:

`Vector3 flat = new Vector3(rb.linearVelocity.x, 0f, rb.linearVelocity.z);`

`Vector3 requested = flat + direction * (speed / rb.mass) * Time.fixedDeltaTime;`

`Vector3 limited = Vector3.ClampMagnitude(requested, maxSpeed);`

`rb.AddForce(limited - flat, ForceMode.VelocityChange);`

The requested velocity includes the change that your original force would produce during the upcoming physics step. `Vector3.ClampMagnitude` limits its length while leaving smaller values unchanged. `ForceMode.VelocityChange` applies the resulting change directly, so this calculation uses `Time.fixedDeltaTime` explicitly. The change has no y component, so jumping and falling still work. Remove the original horizontal force call; leaving it in would add another push after your limit calculation. To check the simulated flat speed, temporarily log it in `Update` with `Debug.Log(new Vector3(rb.linearVelocity.x, 0f, rb.linearVelocity.z).magnitude);`, then remove that line.

For the jump, Space gives one push per press and rolling still works. For the cap, the ball never rolls faster than Max Speed. It went wrong if the jump fires repeatedly while Space is held (you are using isPressed, not wasPressedThisFrame) or if the ball floats when falling (you set the y part of the velocity to 0 in the cap).
Wrap-up

You can now read the keyboard with Keyboard.current or the Move action, push a Rigidbody from FixedUpdate, and write a script that keeps the camera behind the ball. Test yourself. How do you read whether A is held in this project, and why not Input.GetKey? Why is AddForce called in FixedUpdate and not in Update? What does the camera script store in Start, and why does it move in LateUpdate? Next week the arena fills with spinning pickups. You will collect them using triggers and tags, show a score and a win message in TextMeshPro, and finish Orb Collector.

facilitation.announcement: Welcome to this week. The ball stops being a prop and becomes something you control. You will read the keyboard, push the ball with physics, and write a camera script that follows it. The one thing to get right: read keys in Update, apply forces in FixedUpdate, and use the Input System, never Input.GetKey. Post your first forum reply by Thursday. Replies to other students, the self-check quiz and your Weekly builds item are due Sunday night. If anything stays red in the Console, post the exact error text in the forum and I will reply there.
watchFor: Students copy code from web tutorials that use Input.GetAxis or Input.GetKey, then see InvalidOperationException. Reply in the forum with the error text and point them to the Keyboard.current and Move action code on the page.

Compile errors from a script name that differs from its class name, or a missing `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;`. Ask for the first line of the Console error and the file name, and walk through reading it as in last week’s work.
The ball does not move because the Game view was never clicked, Speed is 0 in the Inspector, or PlayerController is not on Player. Ask for a screenshot of the Inspector for Player in Play mode.
Students look for Drag or Angular Drag on the Rigidbody. In this version the fields are Linear Damping and Angular Damping.

The camera script fails with UnassignedReferenceException because Target is empty, or the student made the camera a child of the ball so the view spins. Tell them to drag Player onto Target and to keep the camera outside the ball.
Forum posts that paste a screenshot of code without the error text. Ask for the exact Console message and the line number.

Your Console is clean and the ball moves in all four directions. Check the diagonal: is it the same speed as straight? The normalizing in your code decides that.
Good use of the Move action. Which line in your script now does what the four `if` lines did in the keyboard version?

l_9e49f2c4974f.title: Collisions, triggers and scoring
l_9e49f2c4974f.summary: Collect spinning pickups using triggers and tags, show a score and win message in TextMeshPro; submit Orb Collector as a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. Things pass through it, and Unity still calls OnTriggerEnter in your script. At least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody, and your Player ball already has one.
A tag is a label on an object. Inside OnTriggerEnter, other.CompareTag(“Pickup”) asks whether the thing you touched carries that label, so only pickups count.
A counter is a whole number that starts at 0 and grows by one each time something happens. An if statement runs its block only when a condition is true, such as the counter reaching the target.
Text on screen is a TMP_Text on a Canvas. Your script sets its text property, and you connect it by dragging the object into a field in the Inspector.

vocabulary.definition: A collider with Is Trigger ticked, which lets other objects pass through it while still telling your code that they entered.
A method Unity calls for you, once, when your object’s collider enters a trigger.
A label you put on an object so that code can tell what kind of object it is.
A method that asks whether an object carries a given tag, such as other.CompareTag(“Pickup”).
A line of code that runs its block only when a condition is true.
A whole number, such as score, that starts at 0 and goes up by one each time something happens.
A method that removes an object from the scene.
The type that holds TextMeshPro text, whose text property your script sets to change what the screen shows.
The flat layer that holds on-screen text and buttons so they stay in front of the game.

study.overview: This week you finished Orb Collector. The ball now collects spinning pickups, the game counts them, and the screen shows a score and a win message. You can now make a trigger, detect it in code, pick out the right objects with a tag, count with an if statement, and put text on screen with TextMeshPro. Reread this page before next week, because Dodge builds on the same ideas.

points.heading: Detect a touch with a trigger and OnTriggerEnter
points.explanation: A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. Other objects pass through it, but Unity still calls `OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` in your script. At least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody, and your Player ball already has one. The method name must be spelled exactly, with a capital T and E, or Unity never calls it and gives no warning. Inside it, `other` is the collider you touched. Example: you ticked Is Trigger on the Box Collider of Pickup and put PickupCollector on Player. When the ball rolled into the pickup, the ball passed through it and the Console printed Picked up Pickup. To remove the object, use `Destroy(other.gameObject)`, not `Destroy(other)`, because `other` is only the collider and you want to remove the whole object.

points.heading: Tell pickups apart with a tag, and count with an if statement
points.explanation: A tag is a label on an object. `other.CompareTag("Pickup")` asks whether the thing you touched carries that label, so only pickups count and everything else is ignored. The word in the code and the tag in the Inspector must match exactly, including the capital P. A counter is a whole number that starts at 0: `private int score = 0;`. Each time the if block runs, `score = score + 1;` takes the old value, adds one, and stores it back. A second if, `if (score >= totalPickups)`, runs its block only when the condition is true. Example: with eight tagged pickups and Total Pickups set to 8, the score goes from 0 up to 8, and the win check becomes true only on the eighth pickup. If You win! appears too early, check that Total Pickups reads 8 and count the pickups in the Hierarchy.

points.heading: Show the score and a win message with TMP_Text
points.explanation: On-screen text is a TMP_Text on a Canvas. Add `using TMPro;` at the top of the script, then declare `[SerializeField] private TMP_Text scoreText;`. The field appears in the Inspector, and you connect it by dragging ScoreText from the Hierarchy onto the Score Text field on Player. Your script then sets the words with `scoreText.text = "Score: " + score + " / " + totalPickups;`. Put that line in your own method, `UpdateScoreText`, and call it from Start and after each pickup, so the screen always matches the counter. The win message works the same way: WinText is emptied in Start with `winText.text = "";` and set to `"You win!"` only when the if finds that the score has reached the total. Example: at Score: 2 / 8, six pickups are left and the win text is empty. If you see a NullReferenceException, a field in the Inspector is empty, so drag the text object onto it.

page.text: Last week your ball learned to roll and the camera learned to follow. This week the arena fills with spinning pickups, and the ball gets a job. You will make the pickups spin, detect the ball with a trigger, tell pickups apart with a tag, count them with an if statement, and show a score and a win message in TextMeshPro. By Sunday you will have a finished Orb Collector that you can play from the first pickup to the win message.

page.text: Line by line. `[SerializeField] private float degreesPerSecond = 90f;` makes a number you can change in the Inspector. It starts at 90, so one full turn takes four seconds. `Update` runs once per frame, so the pickup turns a little each frame. `transform.Rotate` turns the object by the three angles you give it, one for each of the X, Y and Z axes. Only the middle one, Y, is not zero. `Time.deltaTime` is the number of seconds the last frame took. Multiplying by it means the pickup turns at the same speed on a fast computer and a slow one. `Space.World` makes the turn happen around the world’s vertical line, so your tilted cube spins like a top instead of tumbling.

Make the pickup a trigger and detect the ball

page.alt: Slides showing a ball passing through a trigger, the OnTriggerEnter line with other highlighted, a Pickup tag label, and an if block that adds one to a score.

Slide 2: the line OnTriggerEnter(Collider other) with the word other highlighted. Slide 3: a pickup with a tag label Pickup and the line other.CompareTag. Slide 4: an if block with a score counter going from 0 to 1.
page.transcript:
Hello. Last week your ball learned to move. This week it gets a job: collecting things. Let me explain three ideas, then you will build them.

First, collisions and triggers. A collider is the shape that physics uses to feel the world. Normally two colliders meet and push each other. Your ball hits the arena wall and stops. A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. It does not push anything. Other objects pass straight through it, but Unity still tells your code that something went in. That is exactly what a pickup needs. The ball rolls through, and your code decides what happens.

The message arrives as a method called OnTriggerEnter. Unity calls it for you, once, when another collider enters the trigger. It hands you a Collider called other, which is whatever came in. One rule: at least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody. Your ball already has one.

Second, tags. The ball cannot yet tell a pickup from anything else it might touch later, like a hazard. A tag is a label you stick on an object. Your code then asks other.CompareTag, with the label in quotation marks. The spelling and the capital letters must match exactly.

Third, the if statement. It says: only run this block when a condition is true. If the thing I touched is tagged Pickup, then destroy it and add one to the score. The score is a counter, a whole number that starts at zero and goes up by one each time. A second if checks whether the counter has reached the target, and if so shows the win message.

To show text on screen you will use TextMeshPro. Your script keeps a TMP_Text, sets its text property, and the screen updates.

Build it one small step at a time, and test after each step.

page.text: A pickup should not push the ball. The ball should pass through it and the game should notice. A trigger does exactly that, and you set it up here before you add any scoring.

In the **Inspector**, find the **Box Collider** section and tick **Is Trigger**.

In the **Project** window, click the Scripts folder inside **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type PickupCollector and press Enter.
Double-click PickupCollector. Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.

In the **Hierarchy**, click Player. In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type PickupCollector and press Enter.

page.text: `void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` is a method with a name Unity already knows. Unity calls it for you whenever the object this script is on moves into a trigger. The spelling and capitals must be exact, or Unity never calls it and nothing tells you why. `other` is a box that holds the collider of whatever you touched. `Debug.Log` prints a message in the Console, and `other.name` is the name of the object you touched. `Destroy(other.gameObject)` removes that whole object from the scene. It is `other.gameObject`, not `other`, because `other` is only the collider, and you want to remove the object that owns it.

You put the script on Player so one counter tracks every pickup the ball collects. Unity can send trigger messages to scripts on both objects involved. Player already has the Rigidbody needed for these trigger interactions.

1. The ball bounces off the pickup. Click Pickup and tick **Is Trigger** in its **Box Collider** section. 2. The ball goes through but nothing prints. Click Player and check that **Pickup Collector (Script)** is listed in the Inspector, and check that the method is spelled OnTriggerEnter with capital T and E. 3. The Console seems empty although you touched the pickup. Look at the three small icons at the top right of the Console. The message icon must be switched on, or ordinary messages are hidden.
Tag the pickups and keep score with an if statement
Right now the ball would destroy anything it touched that is a trigger. A tag lets the code collect only pickups, and a counter lets it count them.

page.text: `private int score = 0;` is the counter. `int` means a whole number, and it starts at 0. `if (other.CompareTag("Pickup"))` runs the block in curly braces only when the object you touched carries the Pickup tag. Anything else is ignored. `score = score + 1;` reads as: take the old score, add one, and store the result back in score. `score >= totalPickups` is true when the score is 8 or more, so the second `if` runs only when the last pickup is collected. `>=` means greater than or equal to. The `+` between text and numbers in `Debug.Log` joins them into one message.
Make eight pickups

The pickups you copy keep the tag, the trigger and the spin script, so you only set where each one goes. In every Position below, replace the middle value, 0.5, with the pickup height you used earlier on this page. These positions form a ring of radius 4 around the middle of the arena. If your arena is smaller than that, keep every pickup inside its walls by choosing smaller numbers in the same pattern.

Only the first pickup works. The copies were made before the tag was set. Click each copy and set its Tag to Pickup. 3. Red message error CS0103: The name ‘scor’ does not exist in the current context. A variable name is misspelled. Click the message, find the line, and match the spelling to the top of the file.
Show the score on screen with TextMeshPro

Players do not read the Console. They read the screen, so you now put the score where the player can see it. Text on screen uses TextMeshPro, and a Canvas is the flat layer that holds all on-screen text and buttons.

page.text: `using TMPro;` lets your script use TextMeshPro types. `TMP_Text` is the type that holds any TextMeshPro text, and marking the field `[SerializeField]` makes it appear in the Inspector so you can drag ScoreText into it. `UpdateScoreText` is a method you wrote yourself. It builds the words and sets `scoreText.text`, and the screen shows the new words. `Start` runs once when the game begins, so the text shows Score: 0 / 8 straight away. Calling `UpdateScoreText();` is how you run your own method.

page.text: You should see Score: 0 / 8 at the top of the Game view when you press Play, and the number going up by one for each pickup. Gone wrong looks like this: the text never changes from what you typed (Score Text is empty or the script is not on Player), or the Console shows a red message.

1. NullReferenceException when UpdateScoreText runs. Stop Play, select Player, and check the Score Text field in Pickup Collector (Script). If it is empty, drag ScoreText from the Hierarchy onto it. 2. error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘TMP_Text’ could not be found. The line `using TMPro;` is missing or misspelled at the top of the file. 3. The text is in the middle of the screen or is tiny. Check the Rect Transform values and Font Size from the steps above, and check the Game view is not set to a very large size.
Show a win message and test the finished game
A game needs to tell the player they have finished. You add a second text object that stays empty until the last pickup is collected, then you test Orb Collector from start to finish.

page.text: The win message is a text object whose words are an empty string, `""`, until the player wins. In `Start`, `winText.text = "";` empties it, so you can leave the words You win! in the Inspector while you edit. When the `if` finds that `score >= totalPickups`, it sets the text to `"You win!"` and the message appears.
Test the whole game

items.text: Click **Play**. Click once inside the **Game** view. Only Score: 0 / 8 should show.
Roll the ball into the pickups one at a time. Each one disappears and the score goes up by one.
Collect all eight. The text reads Score: 8 / 8 and You win! appears.

page.label: OrbCollector-week-checkpoint.zip
page.shows: The finished OrbCollector project: eight tagged, spinning pickups in a ring, the Player with PickupCollector, and ScoreText and WinText on a Canvas.

page.text: Use the checkpoint file only if your own project does not work and you cannot find why. Unzip it (Extract All on Windows, double-click on a Mac) and open the unzipped folder from the Projects screen in Unity Hub. When this part checks out, you are ready for your Weekly builds item.

You should see Score: 0 / 8 at the start, a score that rises with every pickup, and You win! only after the eighth. Gone wrong looks like this: You win! shows from the start (WinText was not emptied, so the script is out of date or Win Text is empty), or it never shows (fewer than eight pickups have the Pickup tag, or Total Pickups is not 8).

1. NullReferenceException when Start sets the win message. Stop Play, select Player, and check the Win Text field in Pickup Collector (Script). If it is empty, drag WinText onto it. 2. You win! appears too early. Click Player and check that Total Pickups reads 8, and count the pickups in the Hierarchy. 3. The ball cannot reach a pickup. It sits outside or inside a wall. Select it and move its Position inside the arena.
Challenges
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: count down. Change the score text so it shows how many pickups are left instead of how many you have. At the start it reads Left: 8. After you collect three it reads Left: 5. The You win! message still appears when the number reaches 0. Test it in your head: with Total Pickups 8 and a score of 3, the text must read Left: 5, and with a score of 8 it must read Left: 0 and show the win message.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Only `UpdateScoreText` needs to change. The number to show is `totalPickups - score`, which is the total minus what you have already collected. You can build the whole message in one line, the same way the current line joins words and numbers with `+`.

Optional challenge: a hazard. Make a red cube named Hazard in the arena and give it a new tag, Hazard, with Is Trigger ticked. When the ball touches it, the ball returns to its starting position and stops moving. With Play off, select Player and note its starting Position. Use those X, Y and Z values in the hint’s Vector3 instead of 0, 0.5, 0 if yours differ. The score stays the same and the hazard stays where it is. Test it in your head: with a score of 3, the ball touches the Hazard, jumps back to the middle, and the text still reads Left: 5. Pickups already collected stay gone.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add an `else if (other.CompareTag("Hazard"))` block after the Pickup block in OnTriggerEnter. Inside it, set the position with `transform.position = new Vector3(0f, 0.5f, 0f);` and stop its travel with `GetComponent<Rigidbody>().linearVelocity = Vector3.zero;`. On the next line, stop its spin with `GetComponent<Rigidbody>().angularVelocity = Vector3.zero;`. Angular velocity describes how fast the Rigidbody rotates. Release the movement keys while testing the reset, because held keys will push the ball again. Remember that the tag must exist before you can set it.
Wrap-up

You can now make a trigger with Is Trigger and detect it with OnTriggerEnter, pick out pickups with CompareTag, count them with an if statement, and show a score and a win message with TMP_Text. Test yourself. Inside OnTriggerEnter, how do you check that the thing you touched is a pickup? What does the if statement do with the counter, and when does it let the win message appear? Which type holds the text on screen, and how does your script reach it? Next time you start Dodge: a hazard that spawns at random positions on a timer that gets faster and faster, and that you destroy when it is no longer needed.

facilitation.announcement: Welcome to the week where Orb Collector gets finished. This week you make spinning pickups, detect the ball with a trigger, tell pickups apart with a tag, count them with an if statement, and show a score and a win message in TextMeshPro. The one thing to get right: the tag in the Inspector and the word in your code must match exactly, Pickup with a capital P, and ScoreText and WinText must be dragged into their fields on Player. Your first forum post is due Thursday. Replies, the self-check quiz and your Weekly builds submission are due Sunday night. If you are stuck, read the Stuck? list first, then post in the forum with your Console message copied in.
watchFor: Students whose pickups disappear but the score never changes. The tag is still Untagged, or the copies were made before tagging. Ask them to post a screenshot of the Tag row and point them to the stuck list.

Students who put PickupCollector on the Pickup instead of the Player, or who forget Is Trigger. The Console stays empty. Ask which object the script is on and whether the ball goes through the pickup.
UnassignedReferenceException for scoreText or winText. Tell them to drag the Canvas objects into the Player’s fields, and to check the script is saved and compiled.

Students on the old Input class or old code copied from the web, such as FindObjectOfType or rb.velocity. Remind them this course uses the Input System and linearVelocity, and send them back to the page’s code.
Submissions where the recording stops before the win message, or shows a Console with red messages. Ask for a recording that goes through all eight pickups.
feedback: Your trigger works well: the ball passes through and the pickup vanishes at the right moment. Next, try changing totalPickups in the Inspector and watch what the text does.
Your score counts correctly, and I can see the if statement does the checking. Say in your own words in the forum what the line `score >= totalPickups` asks.
The win message appears only after the last pickup, which is what you wanted. Check the Console is free of red messages before you record.
I can see the score on screen but not in your recording from the start. Record from pressing Play so the first Score: 0 / 8 is visible.
You named your objects clearly, so Pickup, ScoreText and WinText are easy to find. Keep doing that in the games you design later.
Your tag has a different capital letter from the code, which is why nothing counted. Tags are matched letter by letter, so copy the spelling exactly.
facilitation.atRisk: By Wednesday, check the forum and the submission list for students who have not posted or opened this week’s work. Send each a short private message: ask where they are stuck and point them to the Stuck? list and the checkpoint file. If the same student has missed two weeks in a row, contact them directly and, if there is no reply by Thursday, tell the course coordinator.

keyIdeas: A prefab is a saved copy of a GameObject, with all its components and settings, kept in the Project window. You build the object once, turn it into a prefab, and then make as many copies as you like from it.
Instantiate makes a new copy of a prefab while the game runs. You give it the prefab, a position and a rotation, and a spawner script calls it each time a timer runs out.
A timer is a variable that counts down by Time.deltaTime every frame. When it reaches 0 you act and reset it. Making each reset a little shorter than the last makes the game get faster.

Every object you create costs the game something, so you also remove it. Destroy with a delay removes a hazard once it is no longer needed. Nystrom’s Object Pool chapter shows the other option, reusing objects.

vocabulary.definition: An object saved as an asset in the Project window, with its components and settings, that you can copy into the scene as many times as you like.
The Unity method that makes a new copy of a prefab while the game runs, given a position and a rotation.
To make a new object appear in the game while it runs.
A number that counts down by Time.deltaTime each frame and triggers an action when it reaches 0.
A method that returns a different random number between two values each time you call it.
A rotation value meaning no rotation at all, used when a copy should appear unturned.
The word Unity adds to the name of a copy made by Instantiate, as in Hazard(Clone).
A fixed set of objects that are reused instead of being created and destroyed again and again.

study.overview: This week you started Dodge by building its heart: hazards that appear at random places, come faster and faster, and are cleaned up when they are no longer needed. You can now save an object as a prefab, copy it while the game runs with Instantiate, drive that copying from a timer, and remove each copy with Destroy. Reread this page before next week, when Dodge gets lives, a game over and a restart.

points.heading: A prefab is a saved copy you build once
points.explanation: A prefab is a GameObject saved in the Project window with all its components and settings. You build the object once, then make as many copies as you like. To make one, you drag the object from the Hierarchy into a folder in the Project window. This week you built Hazard as a cube with a Rigidbody and the HazardRed material, set at Position 3, 5, 0. You dragged it into the Prefabs folder and then deleted the Hierarchy copy. The prefab stayed in the folder. If you want to change every future hazard, select Hazard in the Prefabs folder and change it there, not in the scene.

points.heading: Instantiate and a timer spawn copies while the game runs
points.explanation: Instantiate makes a new copy of a prefab during Play. It needs three things: the prefab, a position and a rotation. In the HazardSpawner script the call is `Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity)`, where `Quaternion.identity` means no rotation. The position comes from `new Vector3(x, spawnHeight, 0f)`, with `x` chosen by `Random.Range(-range, range)`, so with range 9 a hazard can appear anywhere from -9 to 9. A timer decides when. Each frame, `timer = timer - Time.deltaTime;` counts down in seconds. When it reaches 0 or less, you spawn a hazard and reset the timer to `interval`. If the Console says the variable hazardPrefab has not been assigned, the Hazard Prefab field on the Spawner is empty: drag the prefab onto it.

points.heading: Shrinking the gap makes the game faster, with a floor
points.explanation: To make Dodge speed up, make each reset a little shorter than the last. After every spawn the script runs `interval = Mathf.Max(minInterval, interval * shrink);` With `shrink` at 0.95, a gap of 1.5 seconds becomes 1.425, then about 1.354, and so on. `Mathf.Max` picks the larger of two numbers, so the gap never drops below `minInterval`, 0.4. Without that floor the gap would shrink toward 0 and hazards would pour out every frame. If the speed-up never seems to happen, check that Shrink reads 0.95 in the Inspector, because a value of 1 or more keeps the gap the same or longer.

points.heading: Destroy cleans up, and an object pool is the other option
points.explanation: Every object you create costs the game something, so you also remove it. Keep the new copy in a variable, `GameObject hazard = Instantiate(...)`, then call `Destroy(hazard, lifetime);`. The second number is a delay: with `lifetime` at 6, that one copy is removed after 6 seconds, and the prefab and the other copies are not touched. Do not write `Destroy(gameObject)` in the spawner, because that would remove the Spawner itself. With cleanup in place, the Hazard(Clone) rows in the Hierarchy stop growing at about fifteen at the busiest. Nystrom (2014), in the Object Pool chapter of Game programming patterns, describes the other option: reuse a fixed set of objects instead of creating and freeing them. The cost is more code to write and keep correct. Dodge keeps to Instantiate and Destroy for simplicity. If they ever cause performance problems, measure the problem before you decide to use a pool.

page.text: Last week Orb Collector could be finished: you collected pickups, kept a score and showed a win message. This week you start Dodge, your second game, and build its heart: a hazard that falls at random places, faster and faster, and is cleaned up when it is no longer needed. You will make a prefab, copy it with Instantiate on a timer, and remove each copy with Destroy. By Sunday you will have a Dodge scene where you slide a player left and right while hazards rain down.

page.text: Orb Collector had a fixed number of pickups that you placed by hand. Dodge cannot work that way: hazards must appear all the time, in places you did not choose, and they must disappear again. This part explains the ideas behind it and sends you to a short reading before you build.

page.title: Version and template
page.text: This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4f1) and the Universal 3D template. Your window title should read Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1), or another 6000.6 version. If your Editor is a different version, open Unity Hub, click Installs, then Install Editor and add Unity 6.6 before you go on, because menu names and code differ between versions. If Dodge is made from another template, do not use it: make a new project from Universal 3D as shown in the next part, or use the starter file given there.

page.caption: A short talk on prefabs, Instantiate and Destroy. The page below says the same in writing.
page.shows: The instructor on camera beside a simple slide. Slide 1: a red cube labeled Hazard with an arrow to a folder labeled Prefabs. Slide 2: three red cubes at different heights, labeled Instantiate. Slide 3: a clock counting down 1.5, 1.4, 1.3 with the word timer. Slide 4: a red cube with a cross over it, labeled Destroy.
page.transcript:
Hello. This week you start Dodge, and Dodge has a problem Orb Collector did not. In Orb Collector you placed every pickup yourself. In Dodge, hazards fall all the time, in places you did not choose. You cannot place them by hand. So you ask the game to do it.

The first idea is the prefab. A prefab is an object saved in your Project window. You build one red cube, give it a Rigidbody and a material, and then drag it into a folder. That saved version is the template. If you later change the template, every new copy changes with it.

The second idea is Instantiate. Instantiate is the line of code that makes a copy of a prefab while the game is running. You give it three things: the prefab, a position and a rotation. For the position, you pick a random number for the left-right place and a fixed height above the screen.

The third idea is the timer. A timer is a number you count down. Every frame you take away Time.deltaTime, which is the time since the last frame. When the number reaches zero, you spawn a hazard and set the timer again. If each reset is a little shorter than the one before, the hazards come faster and faster.

The last idea is Destroy. Every hazard you make stays in the scene until you remove it. A hundred hazards lying on the floor slow the game and clutter the screen. So each hazard is destroyed a few seconds after it appears.

The reading this week shows a different answer: keep a set of objects and reuse them. Dodge does not need that, but you should know it exists. Now go and build.

page.text: Read: the Object Pool chapter

Read the Object Pool chapter in Nystrom, R. (2014). Game programming patterns. Genever Benning. Read it for three things: the problem it solves (a game that creates and removes many objects of the same kind while it runs), the idea of reusing a fixed set of objects instead of making and freeing them, and the cost of that idea (more code to write and keep correct). You will not copy any code from it. Dodge uses `Instantiate` and `Destroy` to keep the code simple. If creating and destroying hazards later causes performance problems, measure those problems before deciding whether to use an object pool. You do need to know what the alternative is.

You can say in one sentence what a prefab is, what Instantiate does and why hazards must be destroyed. You can also say what an object pool does differently. If any of these is unclear, watch the talk again before you build.
Create the Dodge project and build the arena
Dodge is a new game, so it gets a new project that starts from the defaults, and you build a floor and a camera view first so that everything you add later lands in a scene you can see.

Make the player slide left and right

Hazards need something to be dodged by, so you make a Player cube and a short script that slides it along the floor. It reads keys with the Input System, the same way as earlier in the course, because the old Input class throws an error in this version.

items.text: In the top menu, choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**. Type Player and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 0.5, 0.
In the **Project** window, click the Materials folder inside **Assets**. Choose **Assets > Create > Material**, type PlayerBlue and press Enter.

With PlayerBlue selected, find **Surface Inputs** in the **Inspector** and click the color box beside **Base Map**. In the window titled **Color**, click the **Hexadecimal** box, type 1E88E5 and press Enter. Close the window.

shot.shows: The Color window opened from the Base Map color box of the PlayerBlue material. Outline the Hexadecimal box showing 1E88E5. Same on Windows and Mac.

items.text: Drag PlayerBlue from the **Project** window onto Player in the **Hierarchy**.
In the **Project** window, click **Assets**. Choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Scripts and press Enter.
Click the Scripts folder. Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**, type PlayerMover and press Enter.
Double-click PlayerMover to open it in Visual Studio Code. Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.

page.caption: PlayerMover.cs

page.text: Line by line. `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` lets the script use `Keyboard`. `speed` is a number you can change in the Inspector because of `[SerializeField]`. In `Update`, `direction` starts at 0 each frame. `Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed` is true for as long as A is held, so holding A makes direction -1, and D makes it 1. `Vector3 position = transform.position;` copies the position, because you cannot change only the x part of `transform.position` directly. The next line adds the distance moved this frame: direction times speed times `Time.deltaTime`. `Mathf.Clamp(position.x, -9f, 9f)` keeps x between -9 and 9, so the cube stops before the floor edge at 10. The last line writes the new position back.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

The error says the name `Keyboard` does not exist. The line `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` is missing or misspelled. Add it at the top, save and wait for compiling.

The error says InvalidOperationException about the Input class. Something uses `Input.GetKey` or `Input.GetAxis`. Replace it with the `Keyboard.current` lines above.

A message says the script cannot be added because the class cannot be found. The file name and the class name must match exactly: PlayerMover in both, with the same capital letters.
Turn the hazard into a prefab
You need many hazards but want to build only one, so you build it once, save it as a prefab, and let the spawner copy it later.

items.text: In the top menu, choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**. Type Hazard and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 3, 5, 0.
Click **Add Component**, type Rigidbody, choose **Rigidbody** (not Rigidbody 2D) and press Enter.

Drag HazardRed from the **Project** window onto Hazard in the **Hierarchy**.
In the **Project** window, click **Assets**. Choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Prefabs and press Enter.
Drag Hazard from the **Hierarchy** into the Prefabs folder in the **Project** window.
Click the Prefabs folder. A Hazard prefab is listed inside it.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

The Hazard floated and did not fall. The Rigidbody is missing, or Use Gravity is not ticked. Add it from **Add Component** and tick **Use Gravity**.

The Hazard is plain white, not red. Select Hazard in the Prefabs folder. In its Inspector, expand **Mesh Renderer > Materials** and drag HazardRed from the Materials folder onto the material slot. Future copies will use HazardRed.

You changed the Hazard after making the prefab and the Prefabs copy looks old. Click the Hazard in the Prefabs folder and change it there.
Spawn hazards at random positions on a timer
A spawner is an object with a script that makes copies of the prefab for you, so hazards appear without you placing any.

items.text: In the top menu, choose **GameObject > Create Empty**. Type Spawner and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 0, 0.
In the **Project** window, click the Scripts folder. Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**, type HazardSpawner and press Enter.
Double-click HazardSpawner to open it in Visual Studio Code. Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.

page.caption: HazardSpawner.cs

page.text: Line by line. `hazardPrefab` is a slot for the prefab; you fill it in the Inspector. `range`, `spawnHeight` and `interval` are numbers you can tune without touching the code. `timer` has no `[SerializeField]` because only the script uses it. In `Start`, the timer begins at `interval`. In `Update`, `timer = timer - Time.deltaTime;` takes the time since the last frame off the timer, so it counts down in seconds. When it reaches 0 or less, the `if` block runs: it calls `SpawnHazard` and sets the timer back to `interval`. `SpawnHazard` is a method, a named block of code you can call from other places; you will write more of them next time. `Random.Range(-range, range)` chooses a random decimal number between -9 and 9. Positions can repeat or be close together. `new Vector3(x, spawnHeight, 0f)` builds a position from three numbers. `Quaternion.identity` means no rotation. `Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity)` makes the copy.

items.text: Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
In the **Hierarchy**, click Spawner. In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type HazardSpawner and press Enter.

In the **Project** window, click the Prefabs folder. Drag Hazard onto the **Hazard Prefab** field of the Hazard Spawner component in the **Inspector**. Or click the small circle at the right end of the field and choose Hazard from the list.

page.title: Checkpoint: spawning
page.text: A new red hazard appears every second and a half, at a different place along the floor, and falls onto it. The Hierarchy gains a Hazard(Clone) row each time, and the hazards pile up because nothing removes them yet. If nothing falls, read the stuck box.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

The Console says UnassignedReferenceException: The variable hazardPrefab of HazardSpawner has not been assigned. The Hazard Prefab field is empty. Drag the Hazard prefab from the Prefabs folder onto it.

The Console says error CS1002: ; expected, with a file name and two numbers in brackets. Open HazardSpawner at the line number shown and add the missing semicolon at the end of that line or the one above it.

Nothing happens and the Console is clear. The Spawner may not have the HazardSpawner component. Click Spawner and check the Inspector lists Hazard Spawner.
Destroy hazards and make spawning faster and faster
Hazards left on the floor clutter the game and slow it down, and Dodge should get harder as you play, so you now remove each hazard after a few seconds and shorten the timer on every spawn.

items.text: In the **Project** window, double-click HazardSpawner to open it in Visual Studio Code.
Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.

page.caption: HazardSpawner.cs

page.text: What changed. Three new numbers: `minInterval`, `shrink` and `lifetime`. In `SpawnHazard`, `Instantiate` returns the new copy, and `GameObject hazard =` keeps it in a variable. `Destroy(hazard, lifetime)` removes that one copy after 6 seconds; the prefab and the other copies are not touched. In `Update`, after each spawn, `interval * shrink` makes the gap 5 percent shorter: 1.5 becomes 1.425, then about 1.354, and so on. `Mathf.Max` picks the larger of two numbers, so the gap never drops below 0.4. Without that floor, the gap would shrink toward 0 and hazards would pour out every frame.

page.title: Why this step
page.text: Destroy with a second number waits that many seconds, then removes the object. Writing `Destroy(gameObject)` inside the spawner would remove the Spawner itself, so the script keeps the copy in `hazard` and destroys that.

page.title: Checkpoint: Dodge so far
page.text: Hazards fall faster and faster, the floor never fills up, and the number of Hazard(Clone) rows stops growing at about fifteen at the busiest. If hazards pile up forever, `Destroy(hazard, lifetime);` is missing. If they come out in a stream, check Min Interval in the Inspector reads 0.4.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

The Console says CS0103: The name ‘hazard’ does not exist in the current context. The line `GameObject hazard = Instantiate(...)` is missing or `Destroy(hazard, lifetime);` sits outside `SpawnHazard`. Put both inside its braces.

Nothing falls after the change. The Hazard Prefab field may have been cleared. Click Spawner and drag the Hazard prefab onto it again.

The speed-up never seems to happen. Check Shrink reads 0.95 in the Inspector. A value of 1 or more keeps the gap the same or longer.

page.label: Dodge-week-checkpoint.zip
page.shows: The Dodge project as it should stand now: the Floor, the camera, the blue Player with PlayerMover, the red Hazard prefab in the Prefabs folder and the Spawner with the finished HazardSpawner script.

page.text: Use the checkpoint file only if your own project will not work, or to compare. Unzip it into a different folder from your own Dodge project, for example Documents/DodgeCheckpoint, so that it does not replace yours. On Windows, right-click the zip file, choose Extract All..., then click Extract. On a Mac, double-click the zip file. To open it, start Unity Hub, click Projects, click Add, choose Add project from disk and pick the unzipped Dodge folder.
Challenges: change what you built
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: random sizes. Make every hazard a random size. Each new hazard is a cube between 0.5 and 1.5 units on every side. Test it in your head: if the random number comes out as 0.5, that hazard is a small cube with Scale 0.5, 0.5, 0.5; if it comes out as 1.2, its Scale is 1.2, 1.2, 1.2. Hazards must still fall, be destroyed after 6 seconds and speed up as before.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Only `SpawnHazard` needs to change. `Random.Range(0.5f, 1.5f)` gives the size. `hazard.transform.localScale = Vector3.one * size;` sets all three scale values at once, because `Vector3.one` is 1, 1, 1 and multiplying it by a number scales each part.

Optional challenge: a bonus drop. Make the Space bar drop one extra hazard straight above the Player. The Spawner’s timer and speed-up must not change. Test it in your head: if the Player is at x = 4 when you press Space, a new hazard appears at 4, 11, 0 and falls, and it is destroyed after 6 seconds like the others.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` at the top and a slot `[SerializeField] private Transform player;` that you fill by dragging Player onto it. In `Update`, test `Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame`, which is true only on the frame the key goes down. Build the position from `player.position.x`, `spawnHeight` and 0, then instantiate and destroy as in `SpawnHazard`.

page.title: Checkpoint: challenges
page.text: For the first challenge, hazards of clearly different sizes fall, and none stays on the floor for more than about 6 seconds. For the optional one, pressing Space once makes exactly one extra hazard appear above the Player. Hazards can land on the Player, rest on it or slide off. They still disappear when their lifetime ends. Hits are handled later in the course.
Wrap-up

You can now save an object as a prefab, copy it with Instantiate on a timer at random positions, and remove each copy with Destroy. Test yourself. What do you drag, and where, to make a prefab? What are the three things Instantiate needs, and what makes the gap between spawns shrink? Why do hazards need Destroy, and what does an object pool do instead? Next time you add lives, a game over and a restart, using methods and buttons, so Dodge can be lost and replayed. You will submit a recording and screenshot of it, as you did this week.

facilitation.announcement: This week you start Dodge, your second game. You will make a hazard prefab, spawn copies at random positions on a timer that gets faster, and destroy each copy after a few seconds. Read the Object Pool chapter in Nystrom, R. (2014). Game programming patterns. Genever Benning, before you build. The one thing to get right: the Spawner’s Hazard Prefab field must hold the prefab from the Prefabs folder, not an object from the Hierarchy. Deadlines: your first forum post by Thursday. Replies, the self-check quiz and the weekly builds work are due Sunday night. If you get stuck, check the Stuck? boxes on the page, then post in the forum with your Console message and I will answer there.

l_facbf674ef99.title: Game state and UI
l_facbf674ef99.summary: Add lives, game over and restart with methods and buttons, so Dodge can be lost and replayed; submit a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: A method is a named block of code that does one job. You write it once and call it from anywhere, so ‘lose a life’ is one short line wherever it is needed.
Game state is what is true about the game right now, such as how many lives are left and whether the game is over. You keep it in variables and change it inside methods.
A Panel holds a group of UI objects. Switching the panel on or off with SetActive shows or hides everything inside it, and a Button’s On Click list calls a public method when it is pressed.
SceneManager.LoadScene rebuilds the scene from its saved file, which resets lives and objects. Time.timeScale is not part of the scene, so you set it back to 1 yourself.

vocabulary.definition: A named block of code that does one job and can be called from anywhere it is allowed.
A word placed before a method or variable so that other scripts can use it.
The word before a method name that means the method gives nothing back.
What is true about the game right now, such as how many lives are left and whether it is over.
A UI rectangle that acts as a container, so showing or hiding it shows or hides everything inside.
A method that switches a GameObject, and everything inside it, on or off.
The speed of game time: 1 is normal and 0 freezes everything that depends on Time.deltaTime.
The list on a Button that names the public methods to call when the button is pressed.
A label on a GameObject that a script can check to tell what kind of object it touched.
A method that rebuilds a scene from its saved file, which resets every object in it.

study.overview: You can now make Dodge something a player can lose and play again. You write your own methods, keep the game’s state in variables, build a small UI with text and a button, and reload the scene. Reread this page before next week, and check yourself against each point by explaining it in your own words.

points.heading: Write a method once, call it anywhere
points.explanation: A method is a named block of code that does one job. You write it once and call it from anywhere. In Dodge, `LoseLife` takes one life away, updates the text and calls `GameOver()` when none are left. The hazard then needs only one line: `gameManager.LoseLife();`. This works because `LoseLife` is `public`, so other scripts can see it. A `private` method such as `GameOver` can only be called from inside GameManager. When a hazard hits the Player, it finds the GameManager with `FindAnyObjectByType<GameManager>()` in `Start`, because a prefab cannot hold an object from the scene.

points.heading: Keep game state in variables, change it in methods
points.explanation: Game state is what is true about the game right now. Dodge keeps two pieces: `lives`, which starts at 3, and the bool `isGameOver`, which is true or false. Methods change them. `LoseLife` runs `lives = lives - 1;`. `GameOver` sets `isGameOver = true;`. The check `if (isGameOver) { return; }` at the top of `LoseLife` stops a late hit from taking a life after the game has ended. Example: with `lives` at 1, one more hit makes it 0, so `GameOver()` runs and the text reads Lives: 0.

points.heading: Build a UI with a Panel and a Button
points.explanation: A Panel is a container for UI objects. Put Game over text and the Restart button inside GameOverPanel, and `gameOverPanel.SetActive(false);` in `Start` hides all of them at once. `SetActive(true);` in `GameOver` shows them. A Button’s On Click () list calls a public method when pressed: you drag the GameManager object into the Object field and choose GameManager > Restart (). If Restart does nothing, check that the On Click row does not read No Function and that the Hierarchy has an EventSystem.

points.heading: Reload the scene and reset time yourself
points.explanation: `SceneManager.LoadScene(SceneManager.GetActiveScene().name);` rebuilds the open scene from its saved file, so lives return to 3 and the hazards are cleared. `Time.timeScale` is not part of the scene, so a reload does not reset it. `GameOver` sets it to 0 to freeze the game, and `Restart` must set it back to 1 with `Time.timeScale = 1f;` before loading. If you leave that line out, the new game starts frozen. Using `Start` to set it to 1 as well gives a second safeguard.

page.text: Last time your hazards started falling and never stopped, so Dodge could not be lost. This week you fix that. You will give the player three lives, write your own methods to lose a life and end the game, show the lives on screen, and add a Game over panel with a Restart button that reloads the scene. By Sunday night you will have a Dodge you can lose, restart and play again, and you will have submitted a recording and screenshot of it.

Write the GameManager script with three methods
Now the game gets a brain. One script, the GameManager, will keep the number of lives and decide when the game is over. Watch the short video first: it explains the two ideas the script uses.

page.alt: GameManager.cs in Visual Studio Code with the methods LoseLife, GameOver and Restart highlighted in turn.
page.caption: Methods and game state, in about three minutes.
page.shows: Instructor’s voice over Visual Studio Code with the finished GameManager.cs open. The three method names LoseLife, GameOver and Restart are highlighted one after another, then the line Time.timeScale = 0f is highlighted as it is mentioned.
page.transcript:
Hello. Last time your hazards started falling and never stopped. This week Dodge learns to end. To do that you need two ideas: methods and game state.

A method is a named block of code that does one job. You already use methods: Start and Update are methods that Unity calls for you. This week you write your own. Suppose I name a method LoseLife. Inside it I take one away from a number called lives, and I update the text on screen. Now any script can say, lose a life, in one short line, and I never copy those instructions anywhere else. If I later want a sound when you lose a life, I change one place.

A method gets the word public in front of it when other scripts need to call it. The hazard script is another script, so LoseLife must be public. A method that only its own script uses can be private. After the method name come brackets. The word void before the name means the method does its job and gives nothing back.

The second idea is game state. State is what is true about the game right now: how many lives you have, and whether the game is over. We keep state in variables. When the lives variable reaches 0, we change the state: isGameOver becomes true, the game over panel appears, and we set Time.timeScale to 0. That value is the speed of game time. At 0, Time.deltaTime becomes 0 and normal physics updates pause. Your spawner’s countdown no longer advances, and falling hazards freeze. Update still runs, so scripts can still read input.

Restart needs one more step. We call SceneManager.LoadScene with the name of the current scene. Unity throws away every object in the scene and builds it again from the saved file. Lives go back to 3 because the script is created fresh. But Time.timeScale is not part of the scene, so we set it back to 1 ourselves.

In the next steps you will write these three methods: LoseLife, GameOver and Restart. Read the code slowly after you type it.

In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 0, 0.
In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder. Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**, type GameManager and press Enter.

Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
