page.caption: GameManager.cs

page.text: Here is what the new lines do. The `using` lines at the top let the script use TextMeshPro (`using TMPro;`) and scene loading (`using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;`). `[SerializeField] private TMP_Text livesText;` makes a box in the Inspector for the lives text, and `gameOverPanel` does the same for the panel. `lives` holds the number of lives, and `isGameOver` is a bool, a variable that is either true or false. It is the game state. In `Start`, `Time.timeScale = 1f;` sets game time to normal speed, `gameOverPanel.SetActive(false);` hides the panel and everything inside it, and `UpdateLivesText();` shows the starting number. `LoseLife` is public so other scripts can call it. Its `if (isGameOver)` check with `return;` stops the method early when the game has already ended. Then `lives = lives - 1;` takes one life away, and the next `if` calls `GameOver()` when none are left. `GameOver` sets the state, shows the panel and freezes time with `Time.timeScale = 0f;`. `Restart` puts time back to 1 and calls `SceneManager.LoadScene` with the name of the scene that is open now. `UpdateLivesText` joins the words Lives: and the number into one piece of text.

page.alt: Inspector for GameManager with the Game Manager script attached and two fields reading None.
page.caption: Compare: the GameManager object has the script attached, with two empty fields to fill later.
page.shows: Unity Editor, Inspector only, GameManager object selected. Name GameManager at the top, Position 0, 0, 0, and the Game Manager (Script) component below it with Lives Text and Game Over Panel reading None and Lives 3. Outline the component.

page.text:
Likely causes if the script will not work.

Console says: error CS1002: ; expected. A semicolon is missing at the end of a line. Double-click the error to open the script in Visual Studio Code at the reported location. Check that line and the preceding line for a missing semicolon.

The script is in the Project window but not on the object. Drag it onto the GameManager object in the Hierarchy again.
Make a hazard take a life when it hits the Player

Nothing yet calls LoseLife. You will write a small script for the hazard that notices when it touches the Player and calls the method you just made. A tag is a label on an object, and the script uses it to tell the Player from the floor.

page.caption: HazardHit.cs

page.text: `private GameManager gameManager;` is a variable that will hold your GameManager script. A hazard is made by Instantiate while the game runs, so you cannot drag a scene object into it in the Inspector. Instead `FindAnyObjectByType<GameManager>()` in `Start` looks through the scene and gives it back. `OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)` is a method that Unity calls for you when this object touches another object that is solid. `collision.gameObject` is the object it touched, and `CompareTag("Player")` is true only if that object has the Player tag. Then `gameManager.LoseLife();` calls your public method, and `Destroy(gameObject);` removes the hazard that hit.

page.title: Why public matters
page.text: A hazard calls a method in another script. That works because LoseLife is public. If it were private, this script could not see it.

The Player has the tag Player, the Hazard prefab shows Hazard Hit (Script), and the Console has no red errors. Nothing visible changes yet, because the GameManager still has empty fields. If the Hazard Hit component is missing, drag the script onto the prefab again.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Likely causes if it does not work.

Console says: UnassignedReferenceException on the GameManager. A field still reads None. Select GameManager and drag LivesText and GameOverPanel into their fields.

Clicking Restart does nothing. The On Click row is empty or reads No Function, or the Hierarchy has no EventSystem. Redo steps 5 to 7, and if the EventSystem is missing choose GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Event System.

The game is frozen after Restart. Time.timeScale was not set back to 1. Check that Restart in your script starts with `Time.timeScale = 1f;`.
Challenges: change what you built
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: a capped extra life. Add a public method `GainLife` to GameManager. Each call gives the player one more life, but the player can never have more lives than the number they started with. To test it, press the H key to call it from `Update`. Test it in your head: if lives is 2 and you press H, the text reads Lives: 3; if lives is 3 and you press H, it stays Lives: 3. Pressing H after the game is over must do nothing.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Hint: Add a variable `[SerializeField] private int maxLives = 3;`. In `GainLife`, return early if `isGameOver`, then write `lives = Mathf.Min(lives + 1, maxLives);` and call `UpdateLivesText();`. In `Update`, read the key with `Keyboard.current.hKey.wasPressedThisFrame` and add `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` at the top. The old Input class throws an error in this version.

Optional challenge: restart with a key. Let the player press R to restart, but only when the Game over panel is showing. Test it in your head: pressing R while lives are left does nothing; after the last life is lost, pressing R gives the same result as clicking Restart.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Hint: `Update` still runs while Time.timeScale is 0, so it can read the key. Check `isGameOver` and `Keyboard.current.rKey.wasPressedThisFrame` together with `&&`, then call `Restart();`.
Wrap-up

You can now write your own methods, keep game state in variables, build a UI with text and a button, and reload a scene. Test yourself. What does the word public let another script do, and why does the hazard need it? Which values make up Dodge’s game state? What does a button’s On Click list do, and why must you set Time.timeScale back to 1 before calling SceneManager.LoadScene? Next time you add free CC0 sound effects and particle bursts to Dodge and tune how it feels. You will submit a recording and screenshot of it again.

facilitation.announcement: Welcome to the new week. This week Dodge becomes a game you can lose and replay: you will add three lives, a Game over panel and a Restart button, and write your own methods to run them. The one thing to get right is time: Game over freezes time with Time.timeScale = 0, so Restart must set it back to 1 before the scene reloads. Post your first forum message by Thursday. Replies to other students and your weekly build, a short screen recording and a screenshot, are due Sunday night. If you are stuck, read the Stuck? list first, then post your Console error text and what you tried in the forum.
watchFor: The game stays frozen after Restart. Students leave out Time.timeScale = 1f in Restart. Reply in the forum with the line to check and why timeScale is not reset by a scene reload.

Students call the old Input class in the challenges and get InvalidOperationException. Remind them to use Keyboard.current and the Input System.
Hazards do not take lives because the Player tag is not set. Ask whether the tag dropdown reads Player.
feedback: Your recording shows the Lives text counting down, the Game over panel and a restart that works. That is exactly the loop this week asked for.

Your screenshot shows the panel but the recording does not show the restart. Record again, and click Restart on camera.
Good use of isGameOver to stop LoseLife running twice. Say in the forum why that check is needed.
Your capped extra life never goes above the start value. Tell the forum how you tested the edge case where lives is already full.

keyIdeas: Game feel is how it feels to control something on screen in real time. The rules can stay the same while sound, effects and tuning change how an action feels.

vocabulary.definition: How it feels to control something on screen in real time, shaped by input, response and polish.
Extra sound and effects that do not change the rules but make the game’s answer easier to notice.
A license where the creator has given up their rights, so the work is free to use without credit.
A sound file that has been imported into Unity.
The component that plays Audio Clips.
A method that plays a clip on top of whatever is already playing, so it does not cut off earlier sounds.
How high or low a sound is, where 1 is normal.
A component that makes and moves many small bits for a short time to create an effect.
A set number of particles released at one instant.
Changing one value at a time, trying it, and deciding which setting feels best.

study.overview: This week you gave Dodge game feel without changing its rules. You can now play a sound from a script with an Audio Source, make a particle burst appear where a hazard hits the Player, and tune values one at a time so a hit is easy to notice. Reread this page before next time, when you add a start menu and your own twist to Dodge.

points.heading: Game feel comes from more than the rules
points.explanation: Game feel, as Swink (2008) describes it in Game feel: A game designer’s guide to virtual sensation, is how it feels to control something on screen in real time. Polish is the sound, effects and tuning that sharpen that feeling. Last time Dodge’s rules were finished, yet a hit was only a number changing in the corner. Adding a thud and an orange burst left the rules the same and made the hit something you can hear and see. You can now name what a change adds. For example: “The hit now makes a sound and a burst, so I notice it without looking at the Lives text.”

points.heading: Play a sound from a script with PlayOneShot
points.explanation: An Audio Clip is a sound file inside Unity, and an Audio Source is the component that plays it. In SoundPlayer, `source.PlayOneShot(clip, volume)` plays the clip on top of anything already playing, so quick repeats do not cut each other off. Setting the clip and calling Play would stop a sound that is still going. Setting `source.pitch = 1f + Random.Range(-pitchVariation, pitchVariation)` before each play makes the same thud sound a little different each time. To trigger a sound, you call a public method from the moment it belongs to. In Dodge, `FindAnyObjectByType<SoundPlayer>().PlayHit();` sits in `LoseLife`, and `PlayGameOver()` sits in `GameOver`.

points.heading: Make a burst and spawn it where something happens
points.explanation: A Particle System makes many small particles. A burst releases a set number of them at one instant, which suits a hit. In HitBurst, Looping is off, Rate over Time is 0, and the Bursts list holds one entry at Time 0 with Count 20. Stop Action is set to Destroy, so each burst removes itself when it finishes. Saved as a prefab, HitBurst can be copied anywhere. In HazardHit, `Instantiate(burstPrefab, transform.position, Quaternion.identity)` creates a copy at the hazard’s position, and `Destroy(gameObject)` then removes the hazard. If the burst does not appear, check that Burst Prefab is filled on the hazard prefab in the Prefabs folder, not on a copy in the Hierarchy.

points.heading: Tune one value at a time and keep notes
points.explanation: Tuning means changing one value, playing, and deciding. Try a value at each end, then choose between them. In Dodge you tried Volume 0.3 and 1, Pitch Variation 0 and 0.3, burst Count 5 and 60, and Start Speed 2 and 12. Your notes record what you noticed and the value you kept. Keep notes because changes to scene objects, such as SoundPlayer, are undone when Play stops. Changes to assets, such as the HitBurst prefab, are kept. So type values in with Play off, then press Play to judge. A good result is a hit that is easy to notice but does not hide the next hazard, and you can say how you know it helped. For example: “At Count 60 the burst covered the next hazard, so I chose a smaller count.”

page.text: Last time Dodge gained lives, a Game over panel and a Restart button. The rules are finished, but a hit is silent: the only sign is a number changing in the corner. Then you will tune volume, pitch and burst size until the hit feels right. By Sunday you will have a Dodge you can hear and see.

page.text: Read about game feel and open Dodge

page.text: You are about to change how Dodge feels without changing its rules, so you first need to know what feel is. Start with the reading. Read the opening of Swink, S. (2008). Game feel: A game designer’s guide to virtual sensation. Morgan Kaufmann, where he defines game feel. Read it for one thing: how he describes real-time control of something in a simulated space, and what he means by polish. Stop when you can say both in your own words. You do not need to read the whole book.

page.alt: Slides naming input, response and polish, then Dodge with a hit burst, then the note CC0 means free to use with no credit needed.
page.caption: Watch this before you build: it gives you the three ideas and two rules you will use all week.
page.shows: Slides: first the words Input, Response and Polish one at a time, then the clip of Dodge from the top of this page, then a note reading CC0 = free to use, no credit needed.
page.transcript: Press the jump button in a game and nothing else happens on screen. Now picture the same jump with a little squash, a puff of dust and a soft thump. The rules are identical. The feeling is not. That feeling has a name: game feel. Steve Swink wrote the book on it, the one you read this week. His idea, in my words: game feel is how it feels to control something on screen in real time. Three things matter. First, input: what the player does. Second, response: how quickly and clearly the game answers. Third, polish: extra effects that do not change the rules but make the answer easier to notice and nicer to receive. This week is mostly about polish. In Dodge, a hit already costs a life. That is the rule. But right now the hit is silent, and the only sign is a number changing in the corner. The player has to read text to find out something happened. Sound and particles fix that. A hazard touches the Player. At the same moment, a short thud plays and a burst of orange dots flies out. The player knows without reading that they were hit. Two rules for polish. One: it must happen at the same moment as the cause. If the sound arrives late, the game feels broken. Our scripts will play the sound in the same method that takes the life, so that is taken care of. Two: polish serves the game. If a burst is so big that you cannot see the next hazard, it hurts the player. We will tune for that. Tuning means changing one number, trying it, and deciding. Change one thing at a time, because if you change three, you will not know which one helped. Keep a short note of what you tried. Later this week you will do exactly that with volume, pitch, how many particles appear and how fast they fly. One more thing. Use only sounds you are allowed to use. We will use CC0 files: the creator has given up their rights, so you can use them in your game without credit. Now open Dodge and give it some feel.

page.text: You are adding to the Dodge you built last time, so first check that it still works. If it runs now, any error you meet later is one you just caused, and that makes it much easier to find.

page.text:
Likely causes and fixes:

1. A box called Packages with Errors appears when you open the project with no internet connection. Click Dismiss. It is safe.

2. Red text in the Console. Click the first red line, read the file name and line number at the end, and fix that line in Visual Studio Code. Save and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.

3. You cannot fix it in a reasonable time. Use the starter project below: it is Dodge exactly as it stood at the end of last time.

page.text: Add free CC0 sound files to Dodge

Dodge needs sound files before a script can play anything. You will download two short effects that are free to use, then bring them into your project. CC0 means the creator gave up their copyright, so you may use the sounds in your game without crediting anyone. A sound file inside Unity is called an Audio Clip.

In Unity, in the **Project** window, click the **Assets** folder. In the top menu, choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Sounds and press Enter.

page.text:
Likely causes and fixes:

1. The drag did nothing. In the **Project** window, right-click **Sounds** and choose **Show in Explorer** (Windows) or **Reveal in Finder** (Mac), then drop the files into the folder that opens. Unity imports them in a moment.

2. The files do not appear. Unity reads .wav, .ogg and .mp3. Pick a file in one of those formats.

3. You want a different source. On freesound.org, use the license filter and choose Creative Commons 0 before you download.
Play a sound from a script

A sound file does nothing until something plays it. In Unity an Audio Source is the component that plays Audio Clips, so you will make one object that owns it, and a script that other scripts can ask to play a sound. The hit is the cause; the sound must follow at once, so you will call it from the same method that takes the life.

Double-click SoundPlayer to open it in Visual Studio Code. Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.

page.caption: SoundPlayer.cs

page.text: Line by line. `using UnityEngine;` gives you Unity’s types, such as AudioSource. The `[SerializeField] private AudioSource source;` line makes a box in the Inspector that holds the Audio Source; the AudioClip lines make boxes for your two sounds. `volume` and `pitchVariation` are numbers you can change in the Inspector, and `0.8f` is how a decimal number is written in C#. Pitch is how high or low a sound is: 1 is normal, above 1 is higher and faster, below 1 is lower and slower. `PlayHit` and `PlayGameOver` are public, which is what lets another script call them. They both pass a clip to `PlayClip`, which is private because only this script uses it. In `PlayClip`, `Random.Range(-pitchVariation, pitchVariation)` picks a number between the two limits. Adding it to 1 gives a pitch a little above or below normal, so the same thud does not sound identical every time. `source.PlayOneShot(clip, volume)` plays the clip at that volume on top of anything already playing. The other way, setting the clip and calling Play, would cut off a sound that is still going.
Now connect the sounds to the moments they belong to. GameManager already has the methods that run when a life is lost and when the game ends, so you add one line to each.

items.text: In the **Project** window, double-click **GameManager** to open it. Find the method `LoseLife`. Inside its braces, locate the existing check that returns when the game is over. Immediately after that check, before the line that subtracts a life, type `FindAnyObjectByType<SoundPlayer>().PlayHit();`

shot.shows: Visual Studio Code with GameManager.cs open, showing the LoseLife method with the new first line FindAnyObjectByType<SoundPlayer>().PlayHit(); inside its braces. Outline the new line.

items.text: Find the method `GameOver`. As the first line inside its braces, type `FindAnyObjectByType<SoundPlayer>().PlayGameOver();`
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
Click the **Play** button. Let a hazard hit the Player. Listen for the thud. Keep going until the game over sound plays.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: Each hit plays a thud, with a slightly different pitch each time. When the last life goes, the game over sound plays as well. The Console has no red text. If you hear nothing, see the stuck note below.

page.alt: Editor in Play mode with the Game over panel showing and an empty Console
page.caption: Compare: the Console shows no red messages while the Game view shows the Game over panel.
page.shows: The Editor in Play mode after the last life is lost: the Game view shows the Game over panel, and the Console tab at the bottom is open with no red messages.

page.title: No sound, or a red error
page.text:
Likely causes and fixes:

1. Silence. In the Game view toolbar, check that the **Mute Audio** button is not switched on. Then check your computer’s volume, and that the Volume field on Sound Player (Script) is not 0.

2. Red text reading NullReferenceException. Click the error to see which script caused it. If it points to GameManager, check that the Hierarchy contains an active SoundPlayer object with the SoundPlayer script attached. If it points to SoundPlayer, check that its Source field holds the Audio Source. If Unity reports a missing Audio Clip, fill the Hit Clip and Game Over Clip fields.

3. Red text reading error CS0246 or ‘SoundPlayer’ could not be found. The script file is not named exactly SoundPlayer, or the class inside is spelled differently. Rename the file or fix the spelling, save, and wait for the spinner.
Make a particle burst

A sound tells the player’s ears that something happened; a burst tells their eyes. A Particle System is a component that makes many small bits, called particles, and moves them for a short time. A burst is a set number of particles released at one instant, which is exactly what a hit is. You will build the burst once, then turn it into a prefab so a hazard can create a copy of it wherever it is.

items.text: In the top menu, choose **GameObject > Visual Effects > Particle System**. Type HitBurst and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 1, 0.
In the **Particle System** component, untick **Looping**.
Set **Duration** to 1.
Set **Start Lifetime** to 0.6.
Set **Start Speed** to 6.
Set **Start Size** to 0.2.
Click the color box beside **Start Color**. In the window titled **Color**, click the **Hexadecimal** box, type FF8800 and press Enter. Close the window.

shot.alt: Color window with Hexadecimal FF8800
shot.shows: The window titled Color, with the Hexadecimal box showing FF8800. Outline the Hexadecimal box.

items.text: Scroll down in the Particle System component, click the triangle beside **Emission** to open it, and set **Rate over Time** to 0.
In the **Bursts** list under Emission, click the **+** button. Set **Time** to 0 and **Count** to 20.

shot.alt: Emission module with Rate over Time 0 and a burst at Time 0, Count 20
shot.shows: The Inspector with the Particle System component scrolled to the Emission module, showing Rate over Time 0 and one Bursts row with Time 0 and Count 20. Outline the Bursts row.

items.text: Click the triangle beside **Shape** to open it. Set the **Shape** dropdown to **Sphere** and **Radius** to 0.1.
Scroll to the top of the Particle System component and set **Stop Action** to **Destroy**.

shot.alt: Particle System with Duration 1, Looping off, Start Lifetime 0.6, Start Speed 6, Start Size 0.2, Stop Action Destroy
shot.shows: The top of the Particle System component in the Inspector, showing Duration 1, Looping unticked, Start Lifetime 0.6, Start Speed 6, Start Size 0.2 and Stop Action set to Destroy.

page.title: Why Stop Action
page.text: Stop Action set to Destroy removes the burst from the scene once it has finished, so copies do not pile up while you play.
Now preview it, then save it as a prefab. With HitBurst selected, the Scene view plays the burst. If you missed it, find the small Particle Effect box in the Scene view and click **Restart**.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **HitBurst**. Look at the **Scene** view and watch the burst.
In the **Project** window, open the **Prefabs** folder.
Drag **HitBurst** from the **Hierarchy** into the **Prefabs** folder.

shot.alt: Prefabs folder holding HitBurst and the hazard prefab
shot.shows: The Project window with the Prefabs folder open, showing the new HitBurst prefab beside your hazard prefab. Outline HitBurst.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, right-click **HitBurst** and choose **Delete**, or select it and choose **Edit > Delete**.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.text: The Prefabs folder holds HitBurst, and the Hierarchy no longer shows it. When you selected it earlier, about twenty orange dots flew out of a small point and disappeared within a second. If the dots are pink, see the stuck note below.

page.alt: Scene view with an orange burst of dots spreading from a point
page.caption: Compare: orange dots spread from a point, as in the preview, with HitBurst listed in the Hierarchy.
page.shows: The Scene view only, with HitBurst selected before you delete it from the Hierarchy: a ball of about twenty orange dots spreading outward from one point.

page.title: The burst is missing or looks wrong
page.text:
Likely causes and fixes:

1. Nothing appears. Click **Restart** in the Particle Effect box in the Scene view. Check that Count in the Bursts row is 20 and Rate over Time is 0.

2. The dots are pink. The particle material is missing. At the bottom of the Particle System component, open **Renderer** and set **Material** to **Default-ParticleSystem** using the small circle beside the field.

3. The dots keep repeating. **Looping** is still ticked. Untick it.
Make the hazard spawn the burst when it hits

The burst exists, but nothing creates it yet. The hazard detects when it overlaps the Player and knows its own position, so it can make the burst at that position. You will replace the HazardHit script with a version that keeps its job from last time, taking a life when the hazard touches the Player, and adds one more: creating a copy of HitBurst at the hazard’s position.

items.text: In the **Project** window, open the **Scripts** folder and double-click **HazardHit** to open it in Visual Studio Code.
Select everything (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on a Mac), press Delete, and type the file shown below, exactly as written.
Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac. Switch back to Unity and wait for the compiling spinner to finish.
In the **Project** window, open the **Prefabs** folder and click your hazard prefab, the one that carries the HazardHit script.
In the **Inspector**, find **Hazard Hit (Script)** and drag **HitBurst** from the **Prefabs** folder onto the **Burst Prefab** field.

shot.alt: Hazard Hit (Script) with Burst Prefab set to HitBurst
shot.shows: The Inspector for the hazard prefab with Hazard Hit (Script) showing Burst Prefab set to HitBurst. Outline the Burst Prefab field.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.

page.caption: HazardHit.cs

page.text: What is new is the `burstPrefab` box and the `Instantiate` line. `Instantiate(burstPrefab, transform.position, Quaternion.identity)` makes a copy of the prefab. `transform.position` is where this hazard is, so the burst appears at the hit. `Quaternion.identity` means the copy is not turned. Create the burst, then request the hazard’s removal. `Destroy(gameObject)` schedules removal until after the current Update loop; it does not remove the object immediately. The burst then removes itself when it finishes, because you set its Stop Action to Destroy.

items.text: Click the **Play** button.
Let a hazard hit the Player. Watch where the burst appears and listen for the thud.
Keep playing until the Game over panel appears.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: Every hit now makes an orange burst where the hazard touched the Player, at the same moment as the thud, and the Lives text drops. On the final hit the burst may stay still behind the panel because the game is paused; that is expected. If the hazard still touches the Player but nothing bursts, see the stuck note below.

page.alt: Game view with orange dots around the Player and Lives: 2
page.caption: Compare: an orange burst at the moment of the hit and Lives: 2 in the top left.
page.shows: The Game view only, in Play mode, a moment after the first hit: orange dots spread around the Player and the Lives text reads Lives: 2.

page.title: No burst on a hit
page.text:
Likely causes and fixes:

1. Red text reading UnassignedReferenceException: The variable burstPrefab of HazardHit has not been assigned. The Burst Prefab field is empty on the hazard prefab. Drag HitBurst onto it, as in the steps above.

2. Lives drop and the thud plays, but no burst. The field is filled on a hazard in the Hierarchy but not on the prefab, or the hazard prefab is a different one from the one that spawns. Fill the field on the prefab in the Prefabs folder.

3. Nothing happens on a hit at all. Your hazard may use a different hit method from last time, such as OnCollisionEnter. Open the starter project from the first part, read its HazardHit, and keep the method name it uses.
Tune the feel and keep your tuning notes

Now Dodge makes noise and light, but the first numbers are guesses. Tuning is how a guess becomes a decision. Change one value at a time, play, and write down what you chose. Keep a note on paper or in any notes app, with the value you tried and how it felt. The note matters because changes you make to scene objects while Play is on are undone when Play stops. Changes to assets, such as the HitBurst prefab, are kept. So tune with Play off, then play to judge.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **SoundPlayer**. In **Sound Player (Script)**, set **Volume** to 0.3. Click **Play**, take a hit, then click **Play** to stop. Write down how it sounded.
Set **Volume** to 1 and repeat. Write down how it sounded.
Choose the volume you prefer, type it in the **Volume** field, and write it down.

shot.alt: Sound Player (Script) with the Volume field highlighted
shot.shows: The Inspector for SoundPlayer with Sound Player (Script) open, showing the Volume field. Outline the Volume field.

items.text: Set **Pitch Variation** to 0 and play through a few hits. Write down how the repeats sound.
Set **Pitch Variation** to 0.3 and play through a few hits. Write down whether it now sounds like different sounds rather than one sound.
Choose the pitch variation you prefer and type it in the **Pitch Variation** field.
In the **Project** window, open **Prefabs** and click **HitBurst**. In the **Inspector**, find **Bursts** under Emission and set **Count** to 5. Play, take a hit, stop, and write down how it looked.
Set **Count** to 60 and repeat. Write down whether the burst now hides the hazards that come next.
Choose the count you prefer and type it in. Then set **Start Speed** to 2, play and write down how it looked, then try 12 and write that down too.

shot.alt: HitBurst prefab in the Inspector with Count and Start Speed visible
shot.shows: The Inspector with the HitBurst prefab selected, showing the Bursts row under Emission with the Count value you chose and Start Speed near the top. Outline Count.

items.text: Choose the Start Speed you prefer and type it in.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.text: You have a short note recording both trial values for each of volume, pitch variation, burst count and Start Speed, what you noticed, and the final value you chose for each. Dodge still plays through to the Game over panel without red text in the Console. A hit should be easy to notice without hiding the next hazard. Your notes explain whether pitch variation made repeated hits feel better.

page.alt: SoundPlayer in the Inspector with the final Volume and Pitch Variation and an empty Console
page.caption: Compare: your final values are typed into the fields and the Console is empty.
page.shows: The Editor with SoundPlayer selected: the Inspector shows Sound Player (Script) with your final Volume and Pitch Variation, and the Console tab at the bottom is open with no red messages.

page.title: Tuning does not stick
page.text:
Likely causes and fixes:

1. A value you typed has gone back. You changed it while Play was on, and scene changes are undone when Play stops. Stop Play, type it again, and save with **File > Save**.

2. The burst looks the same after you changed it. You edited a copy in the Hierarchy instead of the HitBurst prefab. Edit the prefab in the Project window.

3. A number box will not take a negative value. Type the hyphen on your keyboard; a minus sign pasted from a page is rejected.

The project as it should stand at the end of the guided work is below, so one failure does not block you. Unzip it into a new folder named DodgeFeel so that it does not replace your own Dodge. Windows: in File Explorer, right-click the zip, choose Extract All..., change the end of the path to \DodgeFeel and click Extract. Mac: in Finder, double-click the zip, then rename the folder it makes to DodgeFeel. To open it: in Unity Hub, click Projects, click the arrow beside Add, choose Add project from disk, select the DodgeFeel folder, then click the project in the list.

page.label: Dodge-feel-checkpoint.zip
page.shows: The Dodge project with the SoundPlayer object, HitSound and GameOverSound in the Sounds folder, the HitBurst prefab, the updated GameManager and HazardHit scripts, and tuned starting values for volume, pitch variation and burst count.

page.text: Challenges: change what you built
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: one sound on the last hit. Right now the last hit plays the hit thud and the game over sound together. Change Dodge so that a hit that leaves lives above 0 plays only the thud, and the hit that takes the last life plays only the game over sound. Test it in your head: with 3 lives, a hit leaves 2 and plays the thud only; a hit that leaves 1 plays the thud only; a hit that leaves 0 plays no thud, and the game over sound plays once.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Hint: In LoseLife, the hit sound line is the first line, before the life is taken away. Move it to below the line that subtracts one from `lives`, and wrap it so that it only runs when `lives` is still above 0, for example `if (lives > 0)`. Leave the game over line in GameOver where it is.

Optional challenge, further: a different thud each time. Download one more short hit sound, import it into Sounds and name it HitSound2. Change SoundPlayer so that each hit plays one of the hit sounds, picked at random. Test it in your head: with two clips in the list, each hit can play either clip, and the same clip may repeat; with one clip in the list, every hit plays that one; the game over sound is not affected.

page.title: Hint for the optional challenge
page.text: Hint: Replace the single hit clip with a list of clips: `[SerializeField] private AudioClip[] hitClips;`. In the Inspector the list has a Size box; set it to 2 and drag in both sounds. In PlayHit, pick one with `hitClips[Random.Range(0, hitClips.Length)]`. For whole numbers, Random.Range does not include the top number, so the pick is always a valid place in the list. Changing the field removes the clip you assigned before, so drag it in again.
If you finish the challenges, Dodge still plays through to the Game over panel with no red text. Whatever you changed, you can say in one sentence what a player now notices that they did not before.
Wrap-up

You can now play a sound effect from a script with an Audio Source, make a particle burst appear where a hazard hits, and tune values one at a time. Test yourself. Why does PlayOneShot suit a sound that may repeat quickly? What makes a burst a burst, and why is it saved as a prefab? What did you change to make a hit feel better, and how do you know it helped? Next time you add a start menu, build a version a classmate can run, and add your own twist to Dodge. You will submit the finished Dodge, and it will be graded by rubric.

facilitation.announcement: This week Dodge gets sound and particles. Students add two free CC0 sound effects, play them from a script, make an orange burst that appears where a hazard hits the Player, and tune volume, pitch and burst size. The one thing to get right: they change one value at a time and keep a short note of what they tried. Reading: Swink, S. (2008). Game feel: A game designer’s guide to virtual sensation. Morgan Kaufmann. First forum post is due Thursday. Replies, the self-check quiz and the weekly build are due Sunday night. If Dodge from last time will not run, the starter project on the first part gets you moving. Ask in the forum; I will answer there.
watchFor: Silence on a hit. Usually the Mute Audio button in the Game view is on, Volume is 0, or a field on Sound Player (Script) is empty. Ask for a screenshot of the Inspector and the Console in the forum.

Red text reading UnassignedReferenceException for burstPrefab. The Burst Prefab field is filled on a scene copy but not on the hazard prefab. Point them to the fifth part and ask them to fill it on the prefab in the Prefabs folder.

Students tuning during Play and losing their values when Play stops. Remind them that scene changes are undone and asset changes are kept, and that the note is what they hand in as evidence of tuning.
Students changing several values at once. In the forum, ask which value they think made the difference, and suggest going back and changing only one.
Students who use the old Input class or other old API code in their own additions. Remind them that this version reads keys with Keyboard.current.
Students who download sounds without checking the license. Ask where the file came from and point them to CC0 sources such as Kenney or the CC0 filter on Freesound.
feedback: Your note shows three values tried for volume and the one you chose. Say in a sentence what you heard that made you choose it; that is the part that shows your thinking.
The burst appears at the same moment as the sound and the Lives change. That timing is what makes a hit read as one event.
Your burst is clear but is hiding the hazards that come next. Try a smaller Count or a shorter Start Lifetime and see whether you can still see the next hazard.
The pitch variation is working. Check that it is small enough that the thud still sounds like the same sound.
Your recording shows the hit and the game over sound, but the screenshot does not show the Inspector values. Add a screenshot showing your final settings.
Mark the work complete when the recording shows a sound and a burst on a hit and the screenshot shows the project; mark it incomplete with a short note on what is missing and invite a resubmission.
facilitation.atRisk: By Wednesday, send a direct message to any student who has not posted in the forum or opened the Dodge project since last week. Offer the starter project from the first part and ask what is blocking them. If a student reports that Unity will not install or open, or that their computer cannot run it, ask them to describe the problem in a message and refer them to your institution’s student support service for a loan computer or lab access.

t_ce9a8b87ab10.prompt:
Welcome to the forum. This week you installed Unity, toured the Editor and built a Courtyard from shapes by typing exact numbers. Now tell us how it went, in your own words.

Your first post is due by Thursday. Write a short post of a few sentences that does these three things:

1. Describe your Courtyard. Say which object you are most pleased with, and attach your screenshot or describe what the Game view shows.
2. Tell us about one choice or one problem. It might be a Transform number you had to work out, a setting you changed to fit everything in the Game view, a step in the install that went wrong, or a challenge you tried. Say what you did and why.
3. Name the Editor window you expect to use most this term, and give one reason.

By Sunday night, reply to two classmates. Pick posts that are different from yours. If a classmate shares their Courtyard, compare it with yours. Say one thing that works well in it and one thing you would change, such as a position, a scale or the camera. If a classmate is stuck, try their problem and tell them what happened when you tried your fix. Be specific, and kind.

How posts are graded, every week: full marks for a first post by Thursday that is about your own work and answers the prompt, and two replies by Sunday that each help a classmate go further (say what worked for you, suggest one change, or ask a real question). Late or one-line posts earn half.
followUps: You said the Courtyard needed exact numbers. Pick one object and tell us how you would rebuild it on a friend’s computer from your numbers alone. What would you write down?
Look at a classmate’s Game view next to yours. Which of the three things changed the picture most: camera position and rotation, field of view, or the shape of the Game view? How could you test that?
Which problem from the install or the build took you longest? What did you try first, and what finally worked? Write it as two or three steps a later student could follow.

t_b5ada641dd22.prompt: In Unity Hub, which setup creates the local project for this course?

choices.text: Choose Core, select Universal 3D, and set Project name to Create new local project.
Choose Learning, select Universal 3D, and leave Project name connected to Unity Cloud.
Choose Core, select Universal 2D, and set Project name to Create new local project.
Choose Core, select High Definition 3D, and leave Project name connected to Unity Cloud.

t_b5ada641dd22.explanation: In Unity Hub, open the template dropdown beside the search box and choose Core. Select Universal 3D, then use the Project name dropdown to choose Create new local project. The Learning templates, Universal 2D and High Definition 3D do not match this project setup. Review “Create the Courtyard project and tour the Editor.”

t_77f2885b3038.prompt: You want to find a warning Unity showed while opening your project. Which window should you check?

choices.text: Project, where Unity messages appear.
Inspector, where Unity messages appear.
Hierarchy, where Unity messages appear.
Console, where Unity messages appear.

t_77f2885b3038.explanation: The Console shows messages from Unity and later from your code. The Project window holds files, the Inspector shows settings for the selected object, and the Hierarchy lists objects in the open scene. Review “The six windows you will use every week.”

t_0cb83ea709b9.prompt: A Cube has Scale Y set to 4. What Position Y places it on a flat ground at Y = 0, with its bottom resting on the ground?

choices.text: 0, because Position marks the bottom of the Cube.
1, because Position is one quarter of its height.
2, because Position is half of its height.
4, because Position matches its scaled height.

t_0cb83ea709b9.explanation: A Cube is 1 unit tall at Scale 1, so Scale Y of 4 makes it 4 units tall. Position gives the center, so the center must be half the height above the ground: 4 ÷ 2 = 2. Position is not the bottom or the full height. Review “Build the courtyard from primitive shapes.”

t_0f7ca91a0fb3.prompt: Every GameObject has a Transform with Position, Rotation, and Scale settings.

choices.text: True
False

t_0f7ca91a0fb3.explanation: The Transform stores where an object is, how it is turned, and how big it is. Review “Build the courtyard from primitive shapes.”

t_e40eed3aafac.prompt: Name the three things that work together to determine what appears in the Game view.
t_e40eed3aafac.answer: The camera’s position and rotation, its field of view, and the shape or aspect ratio of the Game view.
t_e40eed3aafac.explanation: The camera’s position and rotation set where it looks. Its field of view sets how wide an angle it sees, and the Game view’s shape affects how much fits across the picture. Review “Frame the camera, press Play and save.”

t_c11bcd7710f0.title: Weekly builds: Courtyard scene
t_c11bcd7710f0.prompt:
You are learning to build and show a scene in Unity. This build gives you practice using the Hierarchy, Inspector, Transform and Game view, and gives you a saved example of your work from this week.

In your Courtyard project, save the scene as Courtyard. Build the courtyard from the page’s primitive shapes and Transform values, then add one primitive of your own with a name and exact Transform values you chose. Set the Main Camera so the Game view shows the courtyard and your addition. Save the scene, take a screenshot of the Unity Editor with the Game view visible, and make a short screen recording showing Play being pressed and stopped. Upload the screenshot and recording to the LMS by Sunday night this week. In your LMS submission, explain the choice you made for your added object and note any help you used, including AI tools.

Your instructor will use the rubric to give feedback on the scene, your own addition and the submitted captures. Your LMS grade is complete or incomplete. A complete submission includes the saved scene, screenshot, recording and explanation.
steps: Save your project’s scene as Courtyard.
Build the courtyard with the primitive shapes and Transform values from this week’s page.
Add one primitive of your own. Give it a name, set its Position, Rotation and Scale, and explain your choice in your LMS submission.
Set the Main Camera so the Game view shows the courtyard and your added object. Save the scene.
Take a screenshot of the Unity Editor with the Game view visible, and record a short clip showing you press Play and stop it.
Upload the screenshot and recording to the LMS by Sunday night this week. Include your explanation and a note of any help you used.

t_ab6921c60e2d.prompt:
This week your shapes stopped being still pictures and started to behave. You gave them color, lit the arena, and added a Rigidbody so a ball could fall and roll. Now show us what you made and what you learned from it.

In your first post, due Thursday, include a screenshot of your Arena (or a short clip of the ball rolling) and tell us three things:

1. One choice you made that was your own. It might be a color you picked for a material or for the light, or a change you made in the challenge. Say why you chose it.
2. One component you switched off, changed or added, and what you saw happen. Name the component, for example Mesh Renderer, Sphere Collider or Rigidbody, and say which job it does: how the object looks, whether it is solid, or whether it moves.
3. One place where you got stuck, or where something surprised you. Say what you tried and what finally worked. If nothing went wrong, tell us what you would warn a new student about.

By Sunday night, reply to two classmates. Look at your classmate’s screenshot or clip and read what they describe. Where you can, try their idea in your own Arena, such as their light color or their way of making a ball bounce. In each reply, say one thing that works well in their scene and one thing you would change, and why. Keep it friendly and specific.

How posts are graded, every week: full marks for a first post by Thursday that is about your own work and answers the prompt, and two replies by Sunday that each help a classmate go further (say what worked for you, suggest one change, or ask a real question). Late or one-line posts earn half.
followUps: You described what happened when you changed a component. Before you pressed Play, what did you expect to see, and how close was it? What does that tell you about which component does which job?
Two of you picked very different light colors for your arena. How does the same slate floor look under each one? What does that show about surface color and light color working together?
If you were stuck, which component in the Inspector did you check first, and what did it tell you? Could a classmate use the same check on a problem of their own?

t_b67eb6e40eb8.title: Weekly builds: components, materials and physics
t_b67eb6e40eb8.prompt:
This build gives you practice using components to change how a GameObject looks and moves. It contributes to Weekly builds, which counts for 40% of your course grade.

In your OrbCollector project, add a sphere named Color_Drop at Position -6, 7, 4. Create a material with a Hexadecimal color you choose and assign it to the sphere. Add a Rigidbody, keep its Sphere Collider enabled and Use Gravity ticked, then press Play to check that it falls and stops on the floor. With Play off, change the Directional Light’s Light Appearance to Color and choose a Hexadecimal color that changes the scene’s look. Save Arena. Take a screenshot of the Unity Editor with the Game view visible, and make a short screen recording showing the sphere fall as you press Play and stop it. Upload both to the LMS by Sunday night this week. In your submission, explain your color choices and note any help you used, including AI tools.

Your instructor will judge the added sphere and its material, the light change, and the screenshot and recording. A complete submission has the saved Arena scene, both captures, and your explanation. The LMS grade is complete or incomplete.
steps: In the OrbCollector project, add a Sphere named Color_Drop. Set Position to -6, 7, 4 and Scale to 1, 1, 1.
Create a new material with a Hexadecimal color of your choice and assign it to Color_Drop. Add a Rigidbody; make sure Use Gravity and the Sphere Collider are enabled.
Set Directional Light’s Light Appearance to Color and choose a Hexadecimal color. Press Play to check that Color_Drop falls and stops on the floor, then stop Play. Save Arena.
Take a screenshot of the Unity Editor with the Game view visible. Make a short screen recording showing you press Play, the sphere fall, and Play stop.
Upload the screenshot and recording to the LMS by Sunday night this week. Include an explanation of your color choices and a note of any help you used, including AI tools.

t_f2b659e6661b.prompt: In one or two sentences, describe what the camera script stores in `Start` and what it does with that value in `LateUpdate`.
t_f2b659e6661b.answer: It stores the offset between the camera and its target in `Start`. In `LateUpdate`, it sets the camera’s position to the target’s current position plus that offset.
t_f2b659e6661b.explanation: The saved offset keeps the camera the same distance from the target as the target moves. `LateUpdate` updates the camera position after the frame’s `Update` methods. Review “Make the camera follow the ball.”

t_28ce3976b133.prompt: In your own words, explain how the spawner removes one hazard copy six seconds after creating it, without removing the prefab or the spawner.
t_28ce3976b133.answer: Store the GameObject returned by `Instantiate` in a variable, then call `Destroy` on that variable with a delay of six seconds, such as `Destroy(hazard, 6f);`.
t_28ce3976b133.explanation: `Instantiate` returns the new copy. Keeping that copy in `hazard` lets the script remove that object after the delay. Calling `Destroy` on the spawner’s `gameObject` would remove the spawner, and destroying the prefab would not be the intended cleanup. Review “Destroy hazards and make spawning faster and faster.”

t_3b5b20f4ff37.title: Weekly builds: Dodge prefabs and spawning
t_3b5b20f4ff37.prompt:
This week you will shape the hazard prefab and show that Dodge can create and remove hazards as play continues. This build contributes to Weekly builds, which counts for 40% of your course grade.

Finish the guided build, then give your hazards a color of your choice and edit `SpawnHazard` so each copy gets a random, uniform scale from 0.8 to 1.2. Keep the timer speed-up and six-second cleanup working. Save the scene, then upload a short screen recording and a screenshot to the LMS by Sunday night. Use MP4 or MOV for the recording and PNG or JPG for the screenshot. Include a brief note explaining your design choices and any help you used, including AI tools.

Your work is graded complete or incomplete. The recording should show hazards appearing at random positions, arriving faster as play continues, and disappearing after a few seconds. The screenshot should show your custom hazard design in the Game view. The note should identify your color and size range and any help used. Proficient or Exemplary work on every rubric criterion is complete.
steps: With Play mode off, choose a color for the Hazard prefab’s material. In `SpawnHazard`, set each new hazard to a random uniform scale between 0.8 and 1.2. Keep the hazards falling and keep the guided timer and cleanup behavior.

Save the scene. Start Play mode and move Player with A and D. Record one run long enough to show hazards appearing at random positions, the gaps between spawns getting shorter, and older hazards disappearing.
Stop Play mode and save the scene. Capture a screenshot of the Game view with your customized hazards visible.
Upload the short screen recording and screenshot to the LMS by Sunday night. Include a brief note stating your chosen color and size range and any help you used, including AI tools.
t_3b5b20f4ff37.answerKey:
1. In `SpawnHazard`, after `GameObject hazard = Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity);`, set `float size = Random.Range(0.8f, 1.2f);` and `hazard.transform.localScale = Vector3.one * size;`. Set the Hazard prefab material’s Base Map color to the student’s stated color. Keep `Destroy(hazard, lifetime);` and the interval update in place.
2. Expected recording: the Player moves with A and D; red or recolored hazards fall at varying x positions; spawn gaps shorten until Min Interval; earlier hazards disappear after the configured lifetime.
3. Expected screenshot: Game view during Play shows the student’s chosen hazard color and more than one visibly different, uniformly scaled hazard.
4. Expected LMS submission: one short MP4 or MOV screen recording, one PNG or JPG screenshot, and a brief note stating the chosen color, size range of 0.8 to 1.2, and any help used, including AI tools.

t_3d8b557e8b5a.prompt:
This week you made Dodge something you can lose and replay. Now tell us how it went for you. In your first post, due Thursday, share a screenshot or a short clip of your Game over panel or your Lives text, and tell us about one choice you made and why. It could be where you put the text, the colors of the panel, how many lives you kept, or how you wrote a method. Then tell us about one moment where you got stuck or something surprised you: what you saw in the Console or in Play mode, what you tried, and what finally worked. If nothing went wrong, tell us what you would change in your game now that it can be lost. By Sunday night, reply to two classmates. Download or open a classmate’s Dodge if they shared it, or follow their description, and try losing and restarting it. In each reply, say one thing that works well and one thing you would change, and say why.

How posts are graded, every week: full marks for a first post by Thursday that is about your own work and answers the prompt, and two replies by Sunday that each help a classmate go further (say what worked for you, suggest one change, or ask a real question). Late or one-line posts earn half.
followUps: You wrote LoseLife and GameOver as separate methods. What would be harder in your project if all that code sat inside the hazard’s collision code instead? Describe one change you might want later, such as a sound when a life is lost, and where you would make it.

Your game state is lives and isGameOver. Is there anything else that is true about your game right now that a player might want to see, such as how long they have survived? Which variable would hold it, and which method would change it?
Describe what a player sees and feels in the second after the last life is lost. Is it clear that the game has ended, and is it clear what to do next? What one change to the panel would improve it?

t_d8a8e30918bb.prompt: In Dodge, a hazard hits the Player while the game is active. Which description best explains how a method helps handle the hit?

choices.text: The hazard changes the scene file, which updates the lives and checks for game over.
The hazard enables the Restart button, which updates the lives and checks for game over.
The hazard changes the text directly, which updates the lives and checks for game over.
The hazard calls the named LoseLife method, which updates the lives and checks for game over.

t_d8a8e30918bb.explanation: A method is a named block of code that does one job. The hazard can call `LoseLife`, which changes the lives and checks whether to call `GameOver`. Changing the scene file is not how the method manages lives. Enabling Restart does not subtract a life or check the game state. Changing text directly would not run the lives and game-over logic. Review “Write the GameManager script with three methods” and “Make a hazard take a life when it hits the Player.”

t_91537a021dcc.prompt: If a UI Panel is turned off with `SetActive(false)`, its child text and button are hidden with it.

choices.text: True
False

t_91537a021dcc.explanation: Turning off the parent Panel hides the UI objects inside it, so one activation change can hide the game-over message and Restart button together. Review “Build the game over panel and the Restart button.”

t_5d2251fa68d2.prompt: Calling `SceneManager.LoadScene` automatically changes `Time.timeScale` back to 1, so `Restart` does not need to set it.

choices.text: True
False

t_5d2251fa68d2.explanation: `Time.timeScale` is not part of the saved scene. If game over set it to 0, `Restart` must set it to 1 before loading the scene. Review “Write the GameManager script with three methods.” The Unity version notes also identify `SceneManager.LoadScene(...)` as the scene-loading method (passage 5).

t_d9521684ee34.prompt: How should you connect the Restart button so it calls the method when pressed?

choices.text: Add the GameManager script asset to On Click and choose GameManager > Restart ().
Add the GameOverPanel object to On Click and choose GameManager > Restart ().
Add the GameManager object to On Click and choose GameManager > Restart ().
Add the GameManager object to On Click and choose GameManager > GameOver ().

t_d9521684ee34.explanation: The button’s On Click list needs the scene object that has the GameManager component, then its public `Restart` method. The script asset is not the scene object with the method to call. The panel does not have the GameManager component. `GameOver` is private and is not the restart action. Review “Connect everything, then play, lose and restart.”

t_85df1c548338.prompt: A hazard hits the Player while one life remains. Describe what `LoseLife` should do next so the game reaches game over.
t_85df1c548338.answer: Subtract one life, update the lives text to 0, then call `GameOver`. `GameOver` marks the game over, shows the panel, and sets `Time.timeScale` to 0.
t_85df1c548338.explanation: `LoseLife` changes the lives variable and refreshes the displayed count. When lives reach 0, it calls `GameOver`, which updates the game state, shows the panel and freezes gameplay. Review “Write the GameManager script with three methods” and “Connect everything, then play, lose and restart.”

t_1a49da7cb81f.title: Weekly builds: Capped extra life
t_1a49da7cb81f.prompt: This build contributes to Weekly builds, which counts for 40% of your course grade. You will extend Dodge so the player can regain a life, while the game enforces a maximum. This gives you practice keeping game state consistent as play changes.
steps: In GameManager, choose a starting number of lives and a different maximum. Add a public GainLife method that returns without changing anything if the game is over, caps lives at your maximum, and updates the lives text. Use the Input System to call GainLife when you press H.
Play Dodge and test your chosen values: show that H adds a life when you are below the maximum, does not go over the maximum, and has no effect after Game over.
Upload a short screen recording and a screenshot of your Game view to the LMS by Sunday night. Include a brief note with your starting lives, maximum lives, and any help you used, including AI tools.

t_9cf44bd8315b.prompt:
This week you gave Dodge a voice and a burst of light, and you tuned them by changing one value at a time. Swink describes game feel as how it feels to control something on screen in real time, and says polish adds to that feeling without changing the rules. Your Dodge now has the same rules as last week, but it should feel different. For your first post, due Thursday, tell us what you made and what you decided. Pick one value you tuned (volume, pitch variation, burst count or Start Speed). Tell us the two trial values you tried, what you noticed with each, and the final value you chose. Say why that final value suits your Dodge, and use your tuning notes to back it up. If you got stuck, say where, and what finally worked. You may also attach a short clip or screenshot of your hit. By Sunday night, reply to two classmates. Download and play their Dodge if they shared it, or watch their clip. In each reply, say one thing that works in how their hit feels and one thing you would change, and say why.

How posts are graded, every week: full marks for a first post by Thursday that is about your own work and answers the prompt, and two replies by Sunday that each help a classmate go further (say what worked for you, suggest one change, or ask a real question). Late or one-line posts earn half.
followUps: You kept the rules the same and changed only sound and effects. Can you point to one moment where a player would act differently, or feel differently, because of that change? What would that tell Swink about where game feel lives?
Your pitch variation or burst count could be bigger or smaller. At what point does a hit stop feeling good and start getting in the way of the next hazard? What would you test to find that point?
If you could add one more piece of feedback to a hit (a screen shake, a flash, a pause), what would it be, and what would you keep one value fixed to compare it fairly?

t_f5a9a375a2a5.title: Weekly builds: Personalized hit feel
t_f5a9a375a2a5.prompt:
This build contributes to Weekly builds, which counts for 40% of your course grade. You will make a personal version of Dodge’s hit effect and use tuning notes to explain your choices. This gives you practice making a game action clearer and more satisfying to play.

Starting from your Dodge project, change the hit burst’s color and tune its particle count and speed. Try two different counts and two different speeds, one value at a time. Keep notes on what you tried, what you noticed, and the final values you chose. Make the result your own by choosing a color and explaining why it suits the hit. Play Dodge and record a short run that shows the effect when a hazard hits the Player. Upload the short screen recording, a screenshot of your Game view, and your tuning notes to the LMS by Sunday night of this week. Include a brief note about any help you used, including AI tools. Common video, image, and text file types work on Windows and Mac.

Your submitted files are graded complete or incomplete. Proficient or Exemplary is complete. The files must show the customized burst in play and your tuning trials, final choices, and reason for your color choice.
steps: In the HitBurst prefab, choose a color for your hit effect that suits your version of Dodge.
With Play off, try a burst count of 12 and then 36. Play after each change and note what you see; choose a final count that makes the hit clear without hiding the next hazard.
Try a Start Speed of 4 and then 9, playing after each change. Note what you see and choose a final speed. Save the prefab and your scene.

Play Dodge and make a short screen recording that shows a hazard hitting the Player with your customized burst. Take a screenshot of the Game view, then upload the recording, screenshot, tuning notes, and a brief note about your color choice and any help used to the LMS by Sunday night of this week.
